chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter is a journey. It starts with how people travelled long ago and today, then uses travel to make large numbers real: the new Ten Thousands place, reading and writing numbers, comparing and rounding them, and finally puzzles that two children play on a train. A short video explains each idea, and an interactive tool lets the student try it alone.

points.title: Videos teach, tools explore
points.text: Every idea has one short concept video. The tool that follows is where the student explores, builds and checks the idea alone, with hints, retry and reset. Eight tools, each with its own purpose, follow the chapter's own plan.

points.title: A tool in three steps
points.text: Each tool opens with a short recall of the video idea, then lets the student play and apply it, and ends with the chapter's own question or puzzle, used exactly as the book gives it.

points.title: Every book question has its own video
points.text: Every solved example, Let Us Do and Let Us Think question and every answerable prompt of the book is its own short video with a step by step solution and a question picture and a solution picture, in a Questions topic that follows the idea it practises.

points.title: One picture for every idea
points.text: Each teaching idea has one clear concept picture: tokens and place value charts, number lines, a digit train, the rabbit and the carrots, the stable. Numbers stay the largest and clearest thing on screen.

points.title: Only the book's facts
points.text: Distances, vehicle sizes and puzzle rules are the book's own. The plan never adds a speed, a fare or a dataset of its own.

concepts.concept_name: My Last Journey

content.text:
When was the last time you went on a long trip? Where did you go? How did you travel? What was the duration of your trip? How much distance did you cover? Ask the elders who went with you to help you answer these questions.
Human beings have always been interested in travelling. About a hundred years ago, there were far fewer vehicles than today. There were animal-drawn carts, cars, and trains. Long before this, thousands of years ago, people travelled long distances on foot or used animals to travel from one place to another. They also built boats and ships to travel across lakes, rivers, and seas. Boats were probably the first form of transport invented by humans, much before bullock carts! Do you know how many vehicles are currently there in your state?

content.text:
1. Predict first: think of your last long trip. Was the distance a 2-digit number of kilometres, a 3-digit number, or more?
2. Every trip is full of numbers: how far you went, how long it took and how many people came with you.
3. Ask the elders who went with you to help you answer. Then wonder: how many vehicles are there in your state?
4. Big journeys and many vehicles need big numbers. We will see how to read and write them.

media.title: Travel Explorer

tool_config.title: Travel Explorer
tool_config.idea: Explore earlier ways of travelling one at a time and sort them into long ago and about a hundred years ago, so the travel story of the chapter is clear before the number lessons begin. The tour ends with an open question about how many vehicles there are in a state, which hands over to big numbers.
tool_config.screen: A warm storybook village by a wide river, drawn as a polished 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation: a dirt road with a bullock cart under trees, a wooden boat and a sailing ship on the river, a footpath, and an old train on a track at the edge of the village. One scene only, no crowd. A row of seven large mode cards runs along the bottom: On foot, Animals, Boat, Sailing ship, Bullock cart, Train and Car. Only one card is active at a time. Tapping a card plays a short use animation in the middle of the scene (a walker crossing the village, animals pulling and carrying, the boat drifting over the river, the ship sailing, the bullock cart rolling, the train moving along the track, a car on the road) and shows one short sentence from the chapter's opening story in a large caption box. When Animals is active, three large chips appear: Animals used for travelling (bullocks, horses, donkeys, mules, elephants), Hilly and snow-covered regions (yaks, dogs, reindeer) and Deserts (camels). A time strip across the top has two labelled bays, Thousands of years ago and About a hundred years ago, and the student drags a mode card into a bay. A counter shows how many of the 7 cards are sorted. Fixed controls: Back and Next in the same places on every card, a Replay button for the animation, a Hint button, a Restart button and progress dots.
student_does: Phase 1, Recall and get ready: look at the village and the river and tap the one way of travelling you think is the oldest.
Phase 2, Play and apply: select one way of travelling at a time, watch it in use, read its short sentence and drag its card into Thousands of years ago or About a hundred years ago.
Phase 3, Challenge: answer the opening questions of the chapter about your own last long trip, and the open question about how many vehicles there are in your state.
challenges: Phase 2, card 1: tap On foot and watch the walker. How did people travel long distances thousands of years ago when they had no animal and no boat? Answer: on foot.

Phase 2, card 2: open Animals and tap each group. Which animals does the story name for hilly and snow-covered regions, and which for deserts? Answer: yaks, dogs and reindeer in hilly and snow-covered regions, and camels in deserts.
Phase 2, card 3: tap Boat and Bullock cart. Which was invented first? Answer: the boat, because boats were probably the first form of transport humans invented, much before bullock carts.

Phase 2, card 4: drag each of the 7 cards into a bay. Answer: Thousands of years ago holds On foot, Animals, Boat and Sailing ship (4 cards). About a hundred years ago holds Bullock cart, Train and Car (3 cards).
Phase 2, card 5: read the counter. How many ways of travelling are sorted in all? Answer: 4 + 3 = 7.

Phase 3, Challenge: 'When was the last time you went on a long trip? Where did you go? How did you travel? What was the duration of your trip? How much distance did you cover?' Ask the elders who went with you, then tap the card that shows how you travelled. Your answer is your own.

Phase 3, Challenge: 'Do you know how many vehicles are currently there in your state?' Guess whether the number has 4 digits, 5 digits or more. Your guess may differ. Next stop: how do we write a number as big as ten thousand?
feedback: Tapping a mode card lights it up, plays its short animation and shows one sentence from the story. Only one card is active at a time.

A card dropped in the right bay locks in with a soft chime and a tick. A card dropped in the wrong bay slides back and shows the story's sentence that places it, for example: About a hundred years ago there were animal-drawn carts, cars and trains.
The counter shows at once how many of the 7 cards are sorted.
The two open questions at the end are never marked wrong: the screen says Your answer may differ and shows Next.
tool_config.done_when: All 7 cards are sorted, the two open questions have been answered once, and the student has pressed Next at the end of the tour.

content.text:
Worked example: The opening story names ways of travelling. Long ago: on foot, on animals, in boats and in ships. About a hundred years ago: animal-drawn carts, cars and trains. How many ways of travelling does the story name in all, and which is older, a boat or a bullock cart?
1. Long ago the story names 4 ways: on foot, on animals, in boats and in ships.
2. About a hundred years ago it names 3 vehicles: animal-drawn carts, cars and trains.
3. Add the two groups: 4 + 3 = 7.
4. The story says boats were probably the first transport humans invented, much before bullock carts.
5. So a boat is older than a bullock cart.
6. Check: foot, animals, boats, ships, carts, cars, trains make 7 names.
Answer: 7 ways of travelling are named, and a boat is older than a bullock cart

concepts.concept_name: What comes after nine thousand?

content.text:
How do you write numbers to show several thousand objects?
Let us start with 1,000. What numbers do we get when we keep adding a thousand?
What number do we get when we add a thousand to 9,000? We get ten thousand. How do we write this number?

lines: How do you write numbers to show several thousand objects?
Let us start with 1,000. What numbers do we get when we keep adding a thousand?
What number do we get when we add a thousand to 9,000? We get ten thousand. How do we write this number?

content.text:
1. Predict first: you keep adding one thousand, 1,000, 2,000, 3,000 and so on. Which number comes after 9,000?
2. Each step adds one more thousand. After 9 thousands, one more thousand makes 10 thousands.
3. 9,000 + 1,000 = 10,000. We say ten thousand.
4. Rule: 10 thousands make 1 ten thousand, and a number with 10 thousands needs a new place.

content.text:
Worked example: Start at 4,150 and keep adding one thousand. Which number do you reach after 9,150, and how do you say it?
1. Add 1,000 each time: 4,150, 5,150, 6,150, 7,150, 8,150, 9,150.
2. The Th place of 9,150 holds 9. One more thousand makes 10 thousands.
3. 9,150 + 1,000 = 10,150.
4. 10 thousands make 1 ten thousand, so write 1 in the new TTh column: 10,150.
5. Say it: ten thousand one hundred fifty.
6. Check: 10,150 − 9,150 = 1,000.
Answer: 10,150, which is ten thousand one hundred fifty

concepts.concept_name: The new TTh column and the value of digits

content.text:
Look at the table below and notice the pattern of writing numbers. In the place value chart, we have added another column, TTh. It stands for ten thousand.
10 Ones = 1 Ten = 10
10 Tens = 1 Hundred = 100
10 Hundreds = 1 Thousand = 1,000
In the same way, 10 Thousands = Ten Thousand = 10,000.
We use a comma to help us read large numbers easily.
Do you remember how we read and write numbers in the Indian place value system? We use the same ten digits 0 to 9 in different places to write larger numbers.
For example, 1,380 = 1 Thousand + 3 Hundreds + 8 Tens + 0 Ones.
9,123 = 9 Thousands + 1 Hundred + 2 Tens + 3 Ones.

content.text:
1. Predict first: the chart has columns O, T, H and Th. Where will the digit for ten thousand go?
2. Ten of one place make one of the next place on its left: 10 ones make 1 ten, 10 tens make 1 hundred, 10 hundreds make 1 thousand, and 10 thousands make 1 ten thousand.
3. So the chart gets a new column, TTh, to the left of Th. Ten thousand is 1 in TTh and 0 in the four places to its right: 10,000.
4. The same ten digits 0 to 9 work in every place. The value of a digit depends on its place: the 3 in 1,380 is 3 hundreds, but the 3 in 9,123 is 3 ones.
5. A comma helps us read a large number. It comes before the last three digits.
6. Rule: ten of one place make one of the next place on the left.

content.text:
Worked example: Put the digits of 52,525 in the place value chart and say what each digit is worth.
1. Write the digits from the left: TTh 5, Th 2, H 5, T 2, O 5.
2. The 5 in TTh is 5 ten thousands: 5 × 10,000 = 50,000.
3. The 2 in Th is 2 thousands: 2 × 1,000 = 2,000.
4. The 5 in H is 5 hundreds: 5 × 100 = 500.
5. The 2 in T is 2 tens: 2 × 10 = 20.
6. The 5 in O is 5 ones: 5 × 1 = 5.
7. Check: 50,000 + 2,000 + 500 + 20 + 5 = 52,525.
Answer: The three 5s are worth 50,000, 500 and 5, and the number is 52,525

concepts.concept_name: Reading and writing large numbers (thousands), the boxes

content.text:
Reading and writing large numbers (thousands), the boxes: Let us start with 1,000. What numbers do we get when we keep adding a thousand? Fill the boxes: 1,000, 2,000, then six empty boxes, then 9,000. What number do we get when we add a thousand to 9,000? How do we write this number?
1. The first box is 1,000 and each box adds 1,000 more.
2. Fill the empty boxes: 3,000, 4,000, 5,000, 6,000, 7,000 and 8,000.
3. Check the last box: 8,000 + 1,000 = 9,000.
4. Add one more thousand: 9,000 + 1,000 = 10,000.
5. 10 thousands make 1 ten thousand, so we say ten thousand.
6. Write 1 in the new TTh column and 0 in Th, H, T and O, with the comma before the last three digits: 10,000.
Answer: The boxes are 1,000 to 9,000, and 9,000 + 1,000 = 10,000, which is ten thousand

concepts.concept_name: Reading numbers beyond ten thousand

content.text:
Let us see how we write numbers beyond 10,000 and how we name them. We write them in the same way as numbers below 9,999. You can use the tokens given in the end of the book.
Tokens 10,000 and 1: number 10,001, TTh 1, Th 0, H 0, T 0, O 1, number name Ten thousand one.
Tokens 10,000, 1 and 1: number 10,002, TTh 1, Th 0, H 0, T 0, O 2, number name Ten thousand two.
Tokens 10,000 and 10: number 10,010, TTh 1, Th 0, H 0, T 1, O 0, number name Ten thousand ten.
Tokens 10,000, two 10s and four 1s: number 10,024, TTh 1, Th 0, H 0, T 2, O 4, number name Ten thousand twenty-four.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a token table shows one 10,000 token and one 1 token. Which number is it, and how do we say it?
2. 10,000 + 1 = 10,001. We say ten thousand one. The zeros hold the Th, H and T places.
3. In the same way, 10,000 + 20 + 4 = 10,024, and we say ten thousand twenty-four.
4. Rule: say the part before the comma and add thousand, then say the hundreds, tens and ones.

content.text:
Worked example: Read the number 34,682 aloud.
1. Put the digits in the chart: TTh 3, Th 4, H 6, T 8, O 2.
2. The part before the comma is 34. Say it and add thousand: thirty-four thousand.
3. H 6 is six hundred.
4. T 8 and O 2 make 80 + 2 = 82, so say eighty-two.
5. Put the parts together: thirty-four thousand six hundred eighty-two.
6. Check: 34,000 + 600 + 82 = 34,682.
Answer: Thirty-four thousand six hundred eighty-two

concepts.concept_name: Reading numbers with zeros

content.text:
1. Predict first: how do you read 10,010? Do you say the zeros?
2. 10,010 has TTh 1, Th 0, H 0, T 1, O 0. The 1 in the Tens place is ten.
3. The zeros hold their places, but we do not say them. So 10,010 is ten thousand ten, not ten thousand one ten.
4. Rule: say only the places that have a digit, and skip every place that holds a zero.

content.text:
Worked example: Read the number 30,402 aloud.
1. Put the digits in the chart: TTh 3, Th 0, H 4, T 0, O 2.
2. The part before the comma is 30. Say it and add thousand: thirty thousand. The 0 in Th is not said.
3. H 4 is four hundred.
4. T 0 means no tens, so say nothing for it. O 2 is two.
5. Put the parts together: thirty thousand four hundred two.
6. Check: 30,000 + 400 + 2 = 30,402.
Answer: Thirty thousand four hundred two

tool_config.title: Number Reading Challenge
tool_config.idea: Read numbers beyond ten thousand by matching the numeral, the number name and the place value tokens: say the part before the comma and add thousand, then the hundreds, tens and ones, and skip every place that holds 0.
tool_config.screen: A large, readable railway station destination board in a warm 3D station scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. The board shows ONE numeral at a time in very large type with its comma; it is the largest thing on screen. Under the board sit three clear panels: a place value chart with the columns TTh, Th, H, T and O, a tray of place value token pictures in the book's colours (10,000 purple, 1,000 green, 100 orange, 10 blue, 1 pink), and a number name strip with empty slots. Below them is a tray of number name word cards (for example Ten, Thirteen, Forty-five, thousand, hundred, one, twenty, twenty-four, five, sixty-seven). Controls: drag a word card into a slot of the name strip, tap a slot to take its card out, a Check button, a Show tokens button that fills the chart and the token tray for the numeral, a Hear it button that says the name aloud, Back and Next in the same places on every card, a Hint button, a Reset button and progress dots. Read-outs: the chart digits light up one column at a time as the matching words are placed, and a counter shows the card number out of 7.
student_does: Phase 1, Recall and get ready: the board shows one 10,000 token and one 1 token. Say aloud the number they make before you touch anything.
Phase 2, Play and apply: for each numeral on the board, drag the word cards into the name strip, then press Show tokens and match the numeral, the name, the chart and the tokens.
Phase 3, Challenge: write the number name for each number of the Number to Name rows in your maths book, using the same board.
challenges: Phase 2, card 1: the board shows 10,001. Build its name. Answer: Ten thousand one (tokens: one 10,000 and one 1).
Phase 2, card 2: the board shows 10,010. Build its name. Answer: Ten thousand ten. The Th, H and O places hold 0 and are not said.
Phase 2, card 3: the board shows the tokens one 10,000, two 10s and four 1s. Tap the numeral that matches and build its name. Answer: 10,024, Ten thousand twenty-four.
Phase 2, card 4: the board shows 13,520. Build its name. Answer: Thirteen thousand five hundred twenty (tokens: one 10,000, three 1,000s, five 100s and two 10s).
Phase 2, card 5: the board shows 45,867. Build its name. Answer: Forty-five thousand eight hundred sixty-seven (tokens: four 10,000s, five 1,000s, eight 100s, six 10s and seven 1s).

Phase 3, Challenge: 'Fill in the blanks appropriately. Use commas as required.' Write the number name for 7,209; 10,599; 13,579; 45,045. Answers: Seven thousand two hundred nine; Ten thousand five hundred ninety-nine; Thirteen thousand five hundred seventy-nine; Forty-five thousand forty-five.

Phase 3, Challenge: 'Fill in the blanks appropriately. Use commas as required.' Write the number name for 39,593; 50,005; 26,050; 81,200. Answers: Thirty-nine thousand five hundred ninety-three; Fifty thousand five; Twenty-six thousand fifty; Eighty-one thousand two hundred.
feedback: A word card dropped in the right slot snaps in and lights the matching column of the chart and the matching tokens. A card in a wrong slot springs back and the column that it should name blinks.
A place that holds 0 stays dark and a small note says there is no word for a zero place.
When the name is complete the board reads it aloud with a short pause at the comma.
A name that is not right points to the part before the comma as the first thing to check, and never shows the full name.
tool_config.done_when: All 7 cards are matched with their numeral, name and tokens, and the last two cards are built correctly without a hint.

concepts.concept_name: Token table (large numbers), first two rows

content.text:
Token table (large numbers), first two rows: Fill in the token table. Write the number and write its digits in the TTh, Th, H, T and O columns. Row 1: the tokens are one 10,000, three 10s and three 1s, and the number name is Ten thousand thirty-three. Row 2: the number is 10,458 and the number name is Ten thousand four hundred fifty-eight; write its digits.
1. Row 1: count the tokens: one 10,000, three 10s and three 1s.
2. Three 10s are 30 and three 1s are 3: 10,000 + 30 + 3 = 10,033.
3. The digits are TTh 1, Th 0, H 0, T 3, O 3, and the name ten thousand thirty-three matches.
4. Row 2: the number is 10,458, so the digits from the left are TTh 1, Th 0, H 4, T 5, O 8.
5. Check with the tokens: 10,000 + 400 + 50 + 8 = 10,458.
Answer: 10,033 has digits 1, 0, 0, 3, 3 and 10,458 has digits 1, 0, 4, 5, 8

Let Us Do (large numbers), Q2 read: Fill in the blanks appropriately. Use commas as required. Write the number name of each of these numbers: 7,209; 10,599; 13,579; 45,045; 39,593; 50,005; 26,050; 81,200.
1. Say the part before the comma and add thousand. Then say the hundreds, tens and ones. Skip every place that holds 0.
2. 7,209: seven thousand, 2 hundreds, 0 tens, 9 ones: Seven thousand two hundred nine.
3. 10,599: Ten thousand five hundred ninety-nine.
4. 13,579: Thirteen thousand five hundred seventy-nine.
5. 45,045: the Hundreds place is 0, so we skip it: Forty-five thousand forty-five.
6. 39,593: Thirty-nine thousand five hundred ninety-three.
7. 50,005: the Th, H and T places are 0, so only the ones are said: Fifty thousand five.
8. 26,050: the Hundreds and Ones places are 0: Twenty-six thousand fifty.
9. 81,200: the Tens and Ones places are 0: Eighty-one thousand two hundred.
10. Check one: 26,000 + 50 = 26,050, which is twenty-six thousand fifty.
Answer: Seven thousand two hundred nine; Ten thousand five hundred ninety-nine; Thirteen thousand five hundred seventy-nine; Forty-five thousand forty-five; Thirty-nine thousand five hundred ninety-three; Fifty thousand five; Twenty-six thousand fifty; Eighty-one thousand two hundred

content.text:
1. Predict first: a ticket says Seventy-two thousand four hundred fifteen. How many digits will its number have, and which digit goes in the TTh place?
2. Find the word thousand. The part before it, seventy-two, gives the TTh and Th digits: 7 and 2.
3. The part after it, four hundred fifteen, gives H 4, T 1 and O 5. The number is 72,415.
4. Rule: write the digits you hear from the left, and put the comma before the last three digits.

concepts.concept_name: Zero holds a place when we write

content.text:
1. Predict first: the name is forty thousand eight. How many digits does the number have, and is it 4,008?
2. Forty thousand is 4 in TTh and 0 in Th. There are no hundreds and no tens. Eight is in the Ones place.
3. Each skipped place needs a 0 so that the digits stay where they belong: the number is 40,008, with 5 digits.
4. Rule: after you place the digits you hear, put 0 in every empty place so that all five places are filled.

tool_config.title: Number Construction
tool_config.idea: Build a number from its name by dropping digit tiles into the TTh, Th, H, T and O slots of a ticket, with a 0 in every place the name skips.
tool_config.screen: A ticket-printing counter in a warm 3D ticket office with soft shadows and gentle animation. A big blank ticket lies on the counter with five large slots labelled TTh, Th, H, T and O and a comma gap before the last three slots; the slots and the number name are the largest things on screen. The number name sits on a strip above the ticket in large type (for example Ten thousand ten). A tray of digit tiles 0 to 9 sits below. Controls: drag a digit tile into a slot, tap a slot to clear it, a Print ticket button that checks the ticket, a Read it back button that shows how the ticket reads as a name, Back and Next in the same places on every card, a Hint button, a Reset button and progress dots. Read-outs: the worth of each placed digit under its slot (for example a 3 in the T slot reads 30), the ticket number with its comma, and a counter of the card number out of 7.
student_does: Phase 1, Recall and get ready: the empty ticket shows TTh, Th, H, T and O. Tap each slot and say what a 1 in it is worth: 10,000, 1,000, 100, 10 and 1.
Phase 2, Play and apply: read the number name on the strip, drag digit tiles into the slots, put 0 in every place the name skips, press Print ticket and compare the ticket with the name.
Phase 3, Challenge: write the number for each name of the Name to Number rows in your maths book, using the same counter.
challenges: Phase 2, card 1: Ten thousand thirty-three. Answer: 10,033 (TTh 1, Th 0, H 0, T 3, O 3).
Phase 2, card 2: Ten thousand four hundred fifty-eight. Answer: 10,458 (TTh 1, Th 0, H 4, T 5, O 8).
Phase 2, card 3: Thirteen thousand five hundred twenty. Answer: 13,520 (the 0 goes in the O slot).
Phase 2, card 4: Twenty thousand. Answer: 20,000 (TTh 2 and a 0 in each of the other four slots).
Phase 2, card 5: Forty-five thousand eight hundred sixty-seven. Answer: 45,867 (TTh 4, Th 5, H 8, T 6, O 7).

Phase 3, Challenge: 'Fill in the blanks appropriately. Use commas as required.' Write the number for Ten thousand seven hundred forty-three; Ten thousand ten; Fifty-six thousand four hundred ninety-one. Answers: 10,743; 10,010; 56,491.

Phase 3, Challenge: 'Fill in the blanks appropriately. Use commas as required.' Write the number for Ninety thousand nine; Twenty-three thousand two hundred thirty; Thirty-six thousand one. Answers: 90,009; 23,230; 36,001.
feedback: A digit tile in a slot shows its worth under it, for example a 3 in the T slot reads 30.
Pressing Print ticket with an empty slot makes the slot blink and says this place needs a digit, use 0 if the name skips it.
A ticket that does not match the name shows the name that the ticket reads as, next to the name asked for, so the student sees the difference without being told the digit.
A correct ticket prints with a stamp and the comma in place before the last three digits.

concepts.concept_name: Finding the rule of a pattern

content.text:
1. Predict first: 120, 135, 150. What is added each time, and what comes next?
2. Find the jump between neighbours: 135 − 120 = 15 and 150 − 135 = 15. The jump is the same, so the rule is add 15.

concepts.concept_name: Patterns that go down or cross ten thousand

content.text:
1. Predict first: 9,700, 9,800, 9,900. What is the next number, and how many digits does it have?
2. The rule is add 100. 9,900 + 100 = 10,000, and the number now has five digits.
3. In a pattern that goes down the numbers get smaller, so the rule subtracts. The pattern 8,400, 8,100, 7,800 subtracts 300 each time, and the next number is 7,800 − 300 = 7,500.
4. Rule: if the numbers grow, add the jump. If they fall, subtract it. Check every pair.

concepts.concept_name: Let Us Do (patterns), Q1 (a) to (c)

content.text:
Let Us Do (patterns), Q1 (a) to (c): Fill in the blanks by continuing the pattern in each of the following sequences. Discuss the patterns in class. (a) 456, 567, 678, then four empty boxes. (b) 1,050, an empty box, 3,150, 4,200, then three empty boxes. (c) 5,501, 6,401, 7,301, then four empty boxes.
1. (a) The jump is 567 − 456 = 111. Check the next pair: 678 − 567 = 111. The rule is add 111.
2. (a) Add 111 each time: 678 + 111 = 789, then 900, 1,011 and 1,122.
3. (b) The jump is 4,200 − 3,150 = 1,050. The empty box is 3,150 − 1,050 = 2,100.
4. (b) Add 1,050 each time after 4,200: 4,200 + 1,050 = 5,250, then 6,300 and 7,350.
5. (c) The jump is 6,401 − 5,501 = 900. Check: 7,301 − 6,401 = 900. The rule is add 900.
6. (c) Add 900 each time: 7,301 + 900 = 8,201, then 9,101, 10,001 and 10,901.
7. Check (c): 10,901 − 7,301 = 3,600 = 4 × 900.
Answer: (a) 789, 900, 1,011, 1,122. (b) 2,100, 5,250, 6,300, 7,350. (c) 8,201, 9,101, 10,001, 10,901

content.text:
Let Us Do (patterns), Q1 (d) to (g): Fill in the blanks by continuing the pattern in each of the following sequences. Discuss the patterns in class. (d) 10,100, 10,200, 10,300, five empty boxes, 10,900 and one more empty box. (e) 10,105, 10,125, then eight empty boxes. (f) 10,992, 10,993, then eight empty boxes. (g) 10,794, 10,796, 10,798, then seven empty boxes.
1. (d) 10,200 − 10,100 = 100, so the rule is add 100: 10,400, 10,500, 10,600, 10,700 and 10,800.
2. (d) Check the printed box: 10,800 + 100 = 10,900. The last box is 10,900 + 100 = 11,000.
3. (e) The jump is 10,125 − 10,105 = 20. Add 20 each time: 10,145, 10,165, 10,185, 10,205, 10,225, 10,245, 10,265 and 10,285.
4. (f) The jump is 10,993 − 10,992 = 1. Add 1 each time: 10,994, 10,995, 10,996, 10,997, 10,998, 10,999, 11,000 and 11,001.
5. (f) 10,999 + 1 = 11,000: the Th digit becomes 1 and the H, T and O digits turn to 0.
6. (g) The jump is 10,796 − 10,794 = 2. Add 2 each time: 10,800, 10,802, 10,804, 10,806, 10,808, 10,810 and 10,812.
7. Check (e): 10,285 − 10,105 = 180 = 9 × 20.
Answer: (d) add 100, the last box is 11,000. (e) add 20, the last box is 10,285. (f) add 1, the last box is 11,001. (g) add 2, the last box is 10,812

content.text:
Let Us Do (patterns), Q1 (h) and (i): Fill in the blanks by continuing the pattern in each of the following sequences. Discuss the patterns in class. (h) 73,005, 72,004, then eight empty boxes. (i) 82,350, 83,350, then eight empty boxes.
1. (h) The numbers fall, so the rule subtracts: 73,005 − 72,004 = 1,001.
2. (h) Subtract 1,001 each time: 72,004 − 1,001 = 71,003, then 70,002, 69,001, 68,000, 66,999, 65,998, 64,997 and 63,996.
3. (h) Check the step across 68,000: 68,000 − 1,001 = 66,999.
4. (i) The numbers grow, so the rule adds: 83,350 − 82,350 = 1,000.
5. (i) Add 1,000 each time: 83,350 + 1,000 = 84,350, then 85,350, 86,350, 87,350, 88,350, 89,350, 90,350 and 91,350.
6. (i) Check: 91,350 − 82,350 = 9,000 = 9 × 1,000.

concepts.concept_name: Which number is greater?

content.text:
1. Predict first: which is greater, 8,965 or 21,304? The first digit 8 is bigger than 2. Does that decide it?
2. Count the digits first. 8,965 has 4 digits and 21,304 has 5 digits.
3. A number with more digits is greater. The 8 in 8,965 is only 8 Thousands, but the 2 in 21,304 is 2 Ten Thousands, worth 20,000.
4. When both numbers have the same number of digits, compare from the left, place by place. Stop at the first place where the digits are different. The bigger digit there makes the greater number.
5. Rule: count the digits first. If they are equal, compare from the left.

1. 8,965 has 4 digits and 21,304 has 5 digits.
2. The number with more digits is greater, so 21,304 is greater than 8,965, even though 8 is bigger than 2.
3. 47,260 and 47,620 both have 5 digits, so compare place by place from the left.
4. The TTh digits are 4 and 4, equal. The Th digits are 7 and 7, equal. The H digits are 2 and 6, different, so stop here.
5. 6 is greater than 2, so 47,620 is greater than 47,260.
Answer: 21,304 is greater than 8,965, and 47,620 is greater than 47,260

concepts.concept_name: Ordering numbers on a number line

content.text:
1. Predict first: on a number line from 0 to 40,000, which will sit farther to the right, 19,780 or 24,305?
2. A number line has equal gaps between its marks. Here the marks are 10,000 apart: 0, 10,000, 20,000, 30,000 and 40,000.
3. To place a number, find the two marks it lies between. 19,780 lies between 10,000 and 20,000. 24,305 lies between 20,000 and 30,000.
4. A number farther to the right is greater. Reading the line from left to right gives the increasing order. Reading it from right to left gives the decreasing order.

content.text:
Worked example: Place 31,250, 8,640, 24,305 and 19,780 on a number line with the marks 0, 10,000, 20,000, 30,000 and 40,000. Then write them in increasing order.
1. The marks are 10,000 apart. Find the two marks each number lies between.
2. 8,640 lies between 0 and 10,000. 19,780 lies between 10,000 and 20,000, just before 20,000.
3. 24,305 lies between 20,000 and 30,000. 31,250 lies between 30,000 and 40,000.
4. Read the line from left to right. The farther a number is to the right, the greater it is.
5. Check with the digits: 8,640 has 4 digits and the others have 5 digits, so it is the smallest.
Answer: 8,640, 19,780, 24,305, 31,250

concepts.concept_name: Numbers between two numbers

content.text:
1. Predict first: how many numbers lie between 71,420 and 72,050? Is there only one?
2. A number between two numbers is greater than the smaller one and less than the bigger one.
3. Look at the leading digits. Both numbers start with 7. The thousands digits are 1 and 2. Keep the leading digits and change a later place to build numbers in between.
4. There are many right answers. Always check the number against the smaller end and the bigger end.
5. A number with 0 in the ones, tens and hundreds places is a whole number of thousands, like 72,000.

content.text:
Worked example: (a) Write three numbers between 71,420 and 72,050. (b) Which of them has 0 in the ones, tens and hundreds places?
1. A number between them must be greater than 71,420 and less than 72,050.
2. Both numbers have 5 digits and start with 7. The Th digits are 1 and 2.
3. Keep Th as 1 and make the hundreds bigger: 71,500 and 71,900 are greater than 71,420 and less than 72,050.
4. Make Th 2 and the hundreds 0: 72,000 is greater than 71,420 and less than 72,050.
5. 72,000 has 0 in the ones, tens and hundreds places.
Answer: 71,500, 71,900 and 72,000 lie between them (many answers are right); 72,000 has zero ones, tens and hundreds

media.title: Which number is greater?
media.context: We the Travellers - I. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Students compare two numbers by counting their digits first, and when the digits are equal they compare place by place from the left, to say which number is greater. It works this example: Which is greater, 8,965 or 21,304? Then which is greater, 47,260 or 47,620?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: which is greater, 8,965 or 21,304? The first digit 8 is bigger than 2. Does that decide it? Count the digits first. 8,965 has 4 digits and 21,304 has 5 digits. A number with more digits is greater. The 8 in 8,965 is only 8 Thousands, but the 2 in 21,304 is 2 Ten Thousands, worth 20,000. When both numbers have the same number of digits, compare from the left, place by place. Stop at the first place where the digits are different. The bigger digit there makes the greater number. Rule: count the digits first. If they are equal, compare from the left. 1. 8,965 has 4 digits and 21,304 has 5 digits. 2. The number with more digits is greater, so 21,304 is greater than 8,965, even though 8 is bigger than 2. 3. 47,260 and 47,620 both have 5 digits, so compare place by place from the left. 4. The TTh digits are 4 and 4, equal. The Th digits are 7 and 7, equal. The H digits are 2 and 6, different, so stop here. 5. 6 is greater than 2, so 47,620 is greater than 47,260. Answer: 21,304 is greater than 8,965, and 47,620 is greater than 47,260

media.description: Concept video: Students place numbers on a number line, read them from left to right to arrange them in increasing order, and read them from right to left to arrange them in decreasing order. It works this example: Place 31,250, 8,640, 24,305 and 19,780 on a number line with the marks 0, 10,000, 20,000, 30,000 and 40,000. Then write them in increasing order.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: on a number line from 0 to 40,000, which will sit farther to the right, 19,780 or 24,305? A number line has equal gaps between its marks. Here the marks are 10,000 apart: 0, 10,000, 20,000, 30,000 and 40,000. To place a number, find the two marks it lies between. 19,780 lies between 10,000 and 20,000. 24,305 lies between 20,000 and 30,000. A number farther to the right is greater. Reading the line from left to right gives the increasing order. Reading it from right to left gives the decreasing order. 1. The marks are 10,000 apart. Find the two marks each number lies between. 2. 8,640 lies between 0 and 10,000. 19,780 lies between 10,000 and 20,000, just before 20,000. 3. 24,305 lies between 20,000 and 30,000. 31,250 lies between 30,000 and 40,000. 4. Read the line from left to right. The farther a number is to the right, the greater it is. 5. Check with the digits: 8,640 has 4 digits and the others have 5 digits, so it is the smallest. Answer: 8,640, 19,780, 24,305, 31,250

media.title: Numbers between two numbers
media.context: We the Travellers - I. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Students write numbers that lie between two given numbers, including numbers whose ones, tens and hundreds digits are all zero, by keeping the leading digits and changing a later place. It works this example: (a) Write three numbers between 71,420 and 72,050. (b) Which of them has 0 in the ones, tens and hundreds places?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: how many numbers lie between 71,420 and 72,050? Is there only one? A number between two numbers is greater than the smaller one and less than the bigger one. Look at the leading digits. Both numbers start with 7. The thousands digits are 1 and 2. Keep the leading digits and change a later place to build numbers in between. There are many right answers. Always check the number against the smaller end and the bigger end. A number with 0 in the ones, tens and hundreds places is a whole number of thousands, like 72,000. 1. A number between them must be greater than 71,420 and less than 72,050. 2. Both numbers have 5 digits and start with 7. The Th digits are 1 and 2. 3. Keep Th as 1 and make the hundreds bigger: 71,500 and 71,900 are greater than 71,420 and less than 72,050. 4. Make Th 2 and the hundreds 0: 72,000 is greater than 71,420 and less than 72,050. 5. 72,000 has 0 in the ones, tens and hundreds places. Answer: 71,500, 71,900 and 72,000 lie between them (many answers are right); 72,000 has zero ones, tens and hundreds

concepts.concept_name: Let Us Do (large numbers), Q3 order

content.text:
Let Us Do (large numbers), Q3 order: Arrange the numbers below in increasing order. You can use the number line below, if required. 40,347, 34,407, 40,473, 34,740, 73,404, 74,430, 47,340, 18,926.
1. All eight numbers have 5 digits, so compare the TTh digits first: 4, 3, 4, 3, 7, 7, 4 and 1.
2. TTh digit 1: 18,926. It is the smallest.
3. TTh digit 3: 34,407 and 34,740. The Th digits are 4 and 4, so compare the H digits, 4 and 7. 34,407 is smaller.
4. TTh digit 4: 40,347, 40,473 and 47,340. The Th digits are 0, 0 and 7, so 47,340 is the greatest of the three.
5. Compare the H digits of the other two, 3 and 4. 40,347 is smaller than 40,473.
6. TTh digit 7: 73,404 and 74,430. The Th digits are 3 and 4, so 73,404 is smaller.
7. Check: on the number line from 0 to 80,000 the eight numbers also sit from left to right in this order.
Answer: 18,926; 34,407; 34,740; 40,347; 40,473; 47,340; 73,404; 74,430

concepts.concept_name: Let Us Do (large numbers), Q4 compare

content.text:
Let Us Do (large numbers), Q4 compare: A student said 9,990 is greater than 49,014 because 9 is greater than 4. Is the student correct? Why or why not? Use the number line below to find the position of the numbers. Fill in the blanks. You can use the place value chart to compare the numbers.
1. Write both numbers in the place value chart. 9,990 is 9 Th, 9 H, 9 T and 0 O. It has 4 digits and the TTh place is empty.
2. 49,014 is 4 TTh, 9 Th, 0 H, 1 T and 4 O. It has 5 digits.
3. A number with more digits is greater, so 49,014 is greater than 9,990.
4. The student compared 9 with 4, but the 9 in 9,990 is in the Th place and the 4 in 49,014 is in the TTh place. Compare first digits only when both numbers have the same number of digits.
5. Fill the number line. The marks are 5,000 apart, so 10,000 − 5,000 = 5,000 and 50,000 − 45,000 = 5,000.
6. The blank marks are 15,000, 20,000, 25,000, 30,000, 35,000, 40,000 and 45,000.
7. 9,990 sits just before the 10,000 mark. 49,014 sits just before the 50,000 mark, much farther to the right.
8. Check: 49,014 is farther to the right than 9,990, so it is greater.
Answer: No, the student is not correct. 49,014 is greater than 9,990 because it has 5 digits and 9,990 has 4. The blanks are 15,000, 20,000, 25,000, 30,000, 35,000, 40,000 and 45,000.

concepts.concept_name: Let Us Do (comparing), Q1 between

content.text:
Let Us Do (comparing), Q1 between: Write 5 numbers between the numbers 23,568 and 24,234.
1. A number between them must be greater than 23,568 and less than 24,234.
2. Both numbers have 5 digits and start with 2. The Th digits are 3 and 4.
3. With Th digit 3 and a bigger hundreds digit, 23,600 and 23,800 are greater than 23,568.
4. With Th digit 4 and a small hundreds digit, 24,000, 24,100 and 24,200 are less than 24,234.
5. Choose five of them: 23,600, 23,800, 24,000, 24,100 and 24,200.
6. Check: 23,568 is less than 23,600, and 24,200 is less than 24,234.
Answer: Sample answer: 23,600; 23,800; 24,000; 24,100 and 24,200. Your answer may differ.

concepts.concept_name: Let Us Do (comparing), Q2 more than and less than

content.text:
Let Us Do (comparing), Q2 more than and less than: Write 5 numbers that are more than 38,125 but less than 38,600.
1. The numbers must be greater than 38,125 and less than 38,600.
2. All of them start with 38, so only the hundreds, tens and ones change. A hundreds digit from 2 to 5 is safe: every such number is greater than 38,125 and less than 38,600.
3. 38,200, 38,300, 38,400 and 38,500 use the hundreds digits 2, 3, 4 and 5.

concepts.concept_name: Let Us Do (comparing), Q4 prices of electric bikes

content.text:
Let Us Do (comparing), Q4 prices of electric bikes: The following are the prices of different electric bikes. Arrange the prices in ascending (increasing) order. ₹90,000, ₹89,999, ₹94,983, ₹49,900, ₹93,743, ₹39,999.
1. All six prices have 5 digits. Compare the TTh digits: 9, 8, 9, 4, 9 and 3.
2. The smallest TTh digit is 3, so ₹39,999 is first. Then 4 gives ₹49,900 and 8 gives ₹89,999.
3. Three prices have TTh digit 9: ₹90,000, ₹94,983 and ₹93,743. Compare their Th digits: 0, 4 and 3.
4. 0 is less than 3 and 3 is less than 4, so the order is ₹90,000, ₹93,743, ₹94,983.
5. Put the parts together: ₹39,999, ₹49,900, ₹89,999, then ₹90,000, ₹93,743 and ₹94,983.
6. Check: 89,999 + 1 = 90,000, so ₹89,999 comes just before ₹90,000.
Answer: ₹39,999; ₹49,900; ₹89,999; ₹90,000; ₹93,743; ₹94,983

concepts.concept_name: Let Us Do (comparing), Q5 population of towns

content.text:
Let Us Do (comparing), Q5 population of towns: The following table shows the population of some towns. Arrange them in a descending (decreasing) order. Town 1 65,232, Town 2 53,231, Town 3 56,380, Town 4 51,336, Town 5 45,858, Town 6 66,540.
1. All six populations have 5 digits. The TTh digits are 6, 5, 5, 5, 4 and 6.
2. The greatest TTh digit is 6: Town 1 (65,232) and Town 6 (66,540). The Th digits are 5 and 6, so Town 6 is greater.
3. TTh digit 5: Town 2 (53,231), Town 3 (56,380) and Town 4 (51,336). The Th digits are 3, 6 and 1, so Town 3 is first, then Town 2, then Town 4.
4. TTh digit 4: Town 5 (45,858) is the smallest.
5. Put the parts together, greatest first: Town 6, Town 1, Town 3, Town 2, Town 4 and Town 5.
6. Check: 66,540, 65,232, 56,380, 53,231, 51,336 and 45,858 each get smaller.
Answer: Town 6 (66,540), Town 1 (65,232), Town 3 (56,380), Town 2 (53,231), Town 4 (51,336), Town 5 (45,858)

concepts.concept_name: Let Us Do (comparing), Q6 zeros in ones, tens and hundreds

content.text:
Let Us Do (comparing), Q6 zeros in ones, tens and hundreds: Find numbers between 42,750 and 53,500 such that the ones, tens, and hundreds digits are all 0.
1. A number with 0 in the ones, tens and hundreds places is a whole number of thousands, like 43,000.
2. The first such number after 42,750 is 43,000, because 42,000 is less than 42,750.
3. The last such number before 53,500 is 53,000, because 54,000 is more than 53,500.
4. List them by adding 1,000 each time: 43,000, 44,000, 45,000, 46,000, 47,000, 48,000, 49,000, 50,000, 51,000, 52,000 and 53,000.
5. Count them: 53 − 43 + 1 = 11 numbers.
6. Check: every number has 0 in the ones, tens and hundreds places, and all lie between 42,750 and 53,500.
Answer: 43,000; 44,000; 45,000; 46,000; 47,000; 48,000; 49,000; 50,000; 51,000; 52,000 and 53,000 (11 numbers)

concepts.concept_name: Swapping two digits changes the value

content.text:
1. Predict first: in 3,925, swap the digits 3 and 9. Will the new number be the same, bigger or smaller?
2. Each digit has a place, and the place gives its value. After the swap, each digit stands in the other digit's place, so its value changes.
3. In 3,925 the 9 is worth 900. After the swap it stands in the thousands place and is worth 9,000. The 3 was worth 3,000 and is now worth 300.
4. Swapping two different digits always changes the number. Swapping two digits that are the same changes nothing.
5. Rule: a bigger digit moving to a bigger place makes the number bigger.

content.text:
Worked example: Swap the digits 3 and 9 in 3,925. Write the new number and say how it compares with 3,925.
1. 3,925 = 3 Thousands + 9 Hundreds + 2 Tens + 5 Ones.
2. Swap the 3 and the 9. The 9 moves to the thousands place and the 3 moves to the hundreds place. The new number is 9,325.
3. The 9 was worth 900 and is now worth 9,000. It gained 9,000 − 900 = 8,100.
4. The 3 was worth 3,000 and is now worth 300. It lost 3,000 − 300 = 2,700.
5. The number changed by 8,100 − 2,700 = 5,400.
6. Check: 9,325 − 3,925 = 5,400, so 9,325 is 5,400 more than 3,925.
Answer: The new number is 9,325. It is 5,400 more than 3,925, so the swap changed the number.

concepts.concept_name: The biggest and the smallest by one swap

content.text:
1. Predict first: in 62,815, which digit should stand in the ten thousands place to make the number as big as it can be?
2. The ten thousands place has the greatest value, so look at it first.
3. To make the biggest number with one swap, bring the biggest digit to the leftmost place. To make the smallest number, bring the smallest digit there.
4. A number cannot start with 0, so never bring a 0 to the front.
5. If the biggest digit is already at the front, leave it and look at the next place.

content.text:
Worked example: Swap two digits of 62,815 to make (a) the biggest number and (b) the smallest number you can with one swap.
1. 62,815 has the digits 6, 2, 8, 1 and 5. The leftmost place, the ten thousands place, matters most.
2. (a) Biggest: the biggest digit is 8. Bring it to the ten thousands place by swapping 6 and 8. The new number is 82,615.
3. (b) Smallest: the smallest digit is 1. Bring it to the ten thousands place by swapping 6 and 1. The new number is 12,865.
4. Check: 82,615 is more than 62,815 and 12,865 is less than 62,815.
Answer: (a) 82,615 (swap 6 and 8). (b) 12,865 (swap 6 and 1).

media.title: Digit Swap Challenge

tool_config.title: Digit Swap Challenge
tool_config.idea: Swapping two digits of a number moves each digit into the other digit's place, so each one takes a new value and the number changes. The student swaps two coaches of a number train, compares the old number with the new number, and chooses swaps to reach a target.
tool_config.screen: A warm, colourful 3D and isometric station with one short railway track, soft shadows and gentle animation. The number train is the largest thing on the screen: each digit of the number is one big coach on the track, the place name (TTh, Th, H, T, O) is painted under each coach, and the whole number with its comma is written large above the train. Below the track two number cards sit side by side, Before and After, with a line that says bigger, smaller or the same and shows the change in value. The task of the card is one short sentence above the train. Controls, all large: tap a coach to select it (a selected coach glows and shows 1 or 2), Swap (the two coaches glide past each other), Undo, Reset, Check, Hint, Back and Next in the same place on every card, and a row of progress dots, one for each of the 6 cards.
student_does: Phase 1, Recall and get ready: the train shows 6,142 with the place name under each coach; before any swap the student predicts whether swapping the first two coaches will make the number bigger, smaller or the same, and then the swap happens.

Phase 2, Play and apply: the student selects two coaches, presses Swap, reads the Before and After cards, and chooses swaps to make a number bigger, smaller, unchanged, the biggest or the smallest, or to land in a given range.
Phase 3, Challenge: the book's digit swap question with the numbers 1,478, 10,593 and 48,247, exactly as the book gives it, shown as a train for each number.
challenges: Play card 1: the train shows 2,614. Swap the coaches 2 and 6 and compare the new number with 2,614. Answer: 6,214, which is bigger, because 6,214 − 2,614 = 3,600.

Two coaches with the same digit show 'These two digits are the same, so the number stays the same.'
A swap that would put 0 at the front shows 'A number cannot start with 0. Try another swap.' and the coaches slide back.
A swap that does not meet the card shows the new number beside the task, for example 'This number is 30,591. The task needs more than 35,000.', and Undo glows.

A correct swap makes the train glow green and names the swap that was made, such as 'You swapped 5 and 2.' If the card has more than one right swap, it adds 'Another swap also works. Can you find it?'
Reset puts the train back to its first number; Back and Next never lose the work on a finished card.

media.title: Swapping two digits changes the value
media.context: We the Travellers - I. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Introduce the digit interchange activity and how swapping digits changes the value of a number. It works this example: Swap the digits 3 and 9 in 3,925. Write the new number and say how it compares with 3,925.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: in 3,925, swap the digits 3 and 9. Will the new number be the same, bigger or smaller? Each digit has a place, and the place gives its value. After the swap, each digit stands in the other digit's place, so its value changes. In 3,925 the 9 is worth 900. After the swap it stands in the thousands place and is worth 9,000. The 3 was worth 3,000 and is now worth 300. Swapping two different digits always changes the number. Swapping two digits that are the same changes nothing. Rule: a bigger digit moving to a bigger place makes the number bigger. 1. 3,925 = 3 Thousands + 9 Hundreds + 2 Tens + 5 Ones. 2. Swap the 3 and the 9. The 9 moves to the thousands place and the 3 moves to the hundreds place. The new number is 9,325. 3. The 9 was worth 900 and is now worth 9,000. It gained 9,000 − 900 = 8,100. 4. The 3 was worth 3,000 and is now worth 300. It lost 3,000 − 300 = 2,700. 5. The number changed by 8,100 − 2,700 = 5,400. 6. Check: 9,325 − 3,925 = 5,400, so 9,325 is 5,400 more than 3,925. Answer: The new number is 9,325. It is 5,400 more than 3,925, so the swap changed the number.

content.text:
Let Us Do (large numbers), Q5 digit swap: Digit swap. (a) In the number 1,478, interchanging the digits 7 and 4 gives 1,748. Now, interchange any two digits in the number 1,478 to make a number that is larger than 5,500. (b) Interchange two digits of 10,593 to make a number (i) between 11,000 and 15,000 (ii) more than 35,000. (c) Interchange two digits of 48,247 to make a number (i) as small as possible (ii) as big as possible.
1. (a) To be larger than 5,500, the thousands digit must be 5 or more. 1,478 has 1 in the thousands place, and its digits are 1, 4, 7 and 8.
2. Bring 7 or 8 to the thousands place: swap 1 and 7 to get 7,418, or swap 1 and 8 to get 8,471.
3. (b)(i) For a number between 11,000 and 15,000, keep 1 in the TTh place and put 1, 2, 3 or 4 in the Th place. 10,593 has 0 in the Th place, so swap 0 and 3 to get 13,590.
4. Swapping 0 with 5 gives 15,093 and swapping 0 with 9 gives 19,503, both too big. So 13,590 is the only way.
5. (b)(ii) The TTh digit of 10,593 is 1. Swapping 1 and 3 gives only 30,591, which is less than 35,000.
6. Bring a bigger digit to the TTh place: swap 1 and 5 to get 50,193, or swap 1 and 9 to get 90,513. Both are more than 35,000.
7. (c)(i) 48,247 has the digits 4, 8, 2, 4 and 7. For the smallest number, bring the smallest digit, 2, to the TTh place by swapping 4 and 2. The new number is 28,447.
8. (c)(ii) For the biggest number, bring the biggest digit, 8, to the TTh place by swapping 4 and 8. The new number is 84,247.
9. Check: 7,418 is more than 5,500; 13,590 is between 11,000 and 15,000; 50,193 is more than 35,000; 28,447 is less than 48,247 and 84,247 is more than 48,247.
Answer: (a) 7,418 or 8,471. (b)(i) 13,590. (b)(ii) 50,193 or 90,513. (c)(i) 28,447. (c)(ii) 84,247.

concepts.concept_name: Expanded form of a number

content.text:
1. Predict first: 5,207 has a 0 in the tens place. Will its expanded form have a tens part?
2. Expanded form breaks a number into the values of its digits. The 5 is in the thousands place, so it is worth 5,000. The 2 is in the hundreds place, so it is worth 200. The 7 is worth 7.

concepts.concept_name: How many tens, hundreds or thousands?

content.text:
1. Predict first: how many ₹10 notes are there in ₹574? Is it the tens digit, 7?
2. No. One ₹10 note is 10, so count how many tens fit. 50 tens make 500 and 7 more tens make 70, so there are 57 tens in 574, with 4 ones left.
3. To count the tens, drop the ones digit. To count the hundreds, drop the last two digits. To count the thousands, drop the last three digits.
4. The same number can be grouped in more than one way. 574 = 57 Tens + 4 Ones, and also 50 Tens + 74 Ones. The number does not change.
5. Two ₹500 notes make 1,000, so count the thousands and double them. Then see if the rest holds one more 500.

content.text:
Worked example: Find the number of tens, hundreds and thousands in 2,745. Write 2,745 as 200 Tens + __ Ones. How many ₹500 notes are there in ₹2,745?
1. Tens: 274 × 10 = 2,740 and 2,745 − 2,740 = 5. So there are 274 tens, with 5 ones left.
2. Hundreds: 27 × 100 = 2,700 and 2,745 − 2,700 = 45. So there are 27 hundreds, with 45 left.
3. Thousands: 2 × 1,000 = 2,000 and 2,745 − 2,000 = 745. So there are 2 thousands, with 745 left.
4. 200 Tens is 2,000 and 2,745 − 2,000 = 745, so 2,745 = 200 Tens + 745 Ones.
5. ₹500 notes: 5 hundreds make one ₹500 note. 27 hundreds hold 5 notes, because 5 × 5 = 25 hundreds and 2 hundreds are left over.
6. Check: 5 × 500 = 2,500, which is less than ₹2,745, and 6 × 500 = 3,000, which is more.
Answer: 274 tens, 27 hundreds and 2 thousands; 2,745 = 200 Tens + 745 Ones; 5 notes of ₹500

content.text:
Let Us Do (place value), Q8 tens and ones: Fill in the blanks with the correct answer. Share your thoughts in class. (a) 983 = 90 Tens + 83 Ones (b) 68 = ___ Tens + 18 Ones.
1. (a) is done: 90 Tens is 900, so the remaining 83 are Ones.
2. (b) The Ones part is 18, so the Tens part is 68 − 18 = 50.
3. 50 is 5 Tens, because 5 × 10 = 50.
4. Check: 5 Tens is 50 and 50 + 18 = 68.
Answer: (b) 5 Tens, so 68 = 5 Tens + 18 Ones.

content.text:
Let Us Do (place value), Q8 hundreds, thousands and ones: Fill in the blanks with the correct answer. (c) 607 = 4 Hundreds + ___ Ones (d) 5,621 = 4 Thousand + ___ Hundreds + 2 Tens + ___ Ones (e) 7,069 = ___ Thousand + 20 Hundreds + ___ Ones (f) 37,608 = ___ Ten Thousand + 17 Thousand + ___ Hundreds + 8 Ones (g) 43,001 = 3 Ten Thousand + ____ Thousand + ____ Hundreds + 1 Ones.
1. (c) 4 Hundreds is 400. 607 − 400 = 207, so the blank is 207 Ones.
2. (d) 4 Thousand is 4,000 and 2 Tens is 20. 5,621 − 4,000 − 20 = 1,601 is left.
3. 1,601 is 16 Hundreds (1,600) and 1 One, so the blanks are 16 Hundreds and 1 Ones.

concepts.concept_name: The nearest ten

content.text:
1. Predict first: a rabbit sits at 4,197. Its food is kept at the two neighbouring tens. Which food will it jump to?
2. The neighbouring tens are the ten just below and the ten just above. For 4,197 they are 4,190 and 4,200.
3. Count the jumps. From 4,197 to 4,200 is 3 jumps. From 4,197 to 4,190 is 7 jumps. Fewer jumps means nearer.
4. The picture also marks the halfway point of the road, 4,195. The rabbit at 4,197 stands on the 4,200 side of it.
5. If the rabbit stood at 4,192, it would be on the 4,190 side. It would need 2 jumps to 4,190 and 8 jumps to 4,200, so it would go down. The nearest ten can be below or above.
6. Do not pick the food that looks most like the number. 4,190 shares more digits with 4,197, but 4,200 is nearer.
7. Rule: the nearest ten is the neighbouring ten with fewer jumps.

content.text:
Worked example: A rabbit is at 4,197. Its food is kept at the neighbouring tens. Which ten is nearest, and how many jumps does the rabbit need?
1. The neighbouring tens of 4,197 are 4,190 and 4,200.
2. Jumps to 4,200: 4,200 − 4,197 = 3.
3. Jumps to 4,190: 4,197 − 4,190 = 7.
4. 3 is less than 7, so 4,200 is nearer. The rabbit stands to the right of the halfway point 4,195, on the 4,200 side.
5. Check: 3 + 7 = 10, the gap between 4,190 and 4,200.
Answer: 4,200 is the nearest ten of 4,197. The rabbit needs 3 jumps.

concepts.concept_name: The nearest hundred and the nearest thousand

content.text:
1. Predict first: a rabbit is at 6,731. Will it go to the same side for the hundreds line and for the thousands line?
2. On the hundreds line the foods are at 6,700 and 6,800. It is 6,731 − 6,700 = 31 jumps to 6,700 and 6,800 − 6,731 = 69 jumps to 6,800.
3. On the thousands line the foods are at 6,000 and 7,000. It is 6,731 − 6,000 = 731 jumps to 6,000 and 7,000 − 6,731 = 269 jumps to 7,000.
4. So the nearest hundred of 6,731 is 6,700, below it, and the nearest thousand is 7,000, above it. Each line has its own two neighbours.
5. Rule: choose the line, find the two neighbours, count the jumps to each and choose the fewer.

concepts.concept_name: Numbers with the same nearest number

content.text:
1. Predict first: can two different numbers have the same nearest hundred? Think of the rabbit and its food.
2. Yes. Each food has numbers on both sides of it that are nearer to it than to any other food. Those numbers share the same nearest number.
3. A number very close to a thousand, such as 8,000, is also close to the nearest hundred and the nearest ten, which are the same 8,000.
4. To check two numbers, count the jumps of each to both of its neighbours on that line.
5. Rule: two numbers have the same nearest number when both are nearer to the same food on that line.

content.text:
Worked example: (a) Write two numbers that have the same nearest hundred. (b) Write two numbers that have the same nearest ten, nearest hundred and nearest thousand.
1. (a) Pick the hundred 5,400 and take one number below it and one above it: 5,380 and 5,420.
2. 5,380 needs 5,400 − 5,380 = 20 jumps to 5,400 and 5,380 − 5,300 = 80 jumps to 5,300. 5,420 needs 5,420 − 5,400 = 20 jumps to 5,400 and 5,500 − 5,420 = 80 jumps to 5,500. Both have the nearest hundred 5,400.
3. (b) Pick the thousand 8,000 and take two numbers very close to it: 7,997 and 8,002.
4. Nearest ten: 7,997 needs 3 jumps to 8,000 and 7,997 − 7,990 = 7 jumps to 7,990. 8,002 needs 2 jumps to 8,000 and 8,010 − 8,002 = 8 jumps to 8,010. Both give 8,000.
5. Nearest hundred: 7,997 needs 3 jumps to 8,000 and 7,997 − 7,900 = 97 jumps to 7,900. 8,002 needs 2 jumps to 8,000 and 8,100 − 8,002 = 98 jumps to 8,100. Both give 8,000.
6. Nearest thousand: 7,997 needs 3 jumps to 8,000 and 7,997 − 7,000 = 997 jumps to 7,000. 8,002 needs 2 jumps to 8,000 and 9,000 − 8,002 = 998 jumps to 9,000. Both give 8,000.
Answer: (a) 5,380 and 5,420, nearest hundred 5,400. (b) 7,997 and 8,002, nearest ten, nearest hundred and nearest thousand all 8,000.

media.title: Rounding Number Line

tool_config.title: Rounding Number Line
tool_config.idea: The nearest ten, hundred or thousand of a number is the neighbouring mark that needs fewer jumps. The student places a rabbit on a milestone road between two neighbouring marks, counts the jumps to each mark and chooses the nearer one.
tool_config.screen: A warm, colourful 3D and isometric countryside with one milestone road, soft shadows and gentle animation. The target number is the largest text, above the road. The road is a straight path drawn as a number line: a carrot (the food) at each end shows the two neighbouring tens, hundreds or thousands, a lit milestone in the middle shows the halfway number, and the student drags a rabbit marker along the road. Read-outs: under the rabbit the number it stands on, under each carrot the jumps to it (shown once the rabbit is placed), and a line Nearest: ___ that fills in after the choice. Controls, all large: a three-button switch Tens, Hundreds and Thousands, tap a carrot to choose it, Check, Hint, Retry, Reset, Back and Next in the same place on every card, and progress dots, one for each of the 7 cards. Only one road is shown at a time. Every target is nearer to one carrot than to the other, so no card ever puts the rabbit on the halfway milestone.
student_does: Phase 1, Recall and get ready: the rabbit stands on a short tens road between two carrots with the halfway milestone lit; the student points to the carrot that looks nearer, and then the jump counts appear to confirm it.

Phase 2, Play and apply: the student picks Tens, Hundreds or Thousands, drags the rabbit to the target number, reads the jumps to the two carrots, taps the nearer carrot, and then repeats on all three roads for one number.

Phase 3, Challenge: the book's rabbit at 2,346 on the tens, hundreds and thousands roads with its blanks to fill, then the book's table of nearest tens, hundreds and thousands for 3,176, 4,017, 5,789 and 8,203.
challenges: Play card 1, nearest ten: the rabbit is at 7,863 and the carrots are at 7,860 and 7,870. Place the rabbit, read the jumps and choose the nearer carrot. Answer: 7,860, 3 jumps (the other carrot needs 7 jumps).
Play card 2, nearest ten: the rabbit is at 3,298 and the carrots are at 3,290 and 3,300. Answer: 3,300, 2 jumps (the other carrot needs 8 jumps).
Play card 3, nearest hundred: the rabbit is at 4,618 and the carrots are at 4,600 and 4,700. Answer: 4,600, 18 jumps (the other carrot needs 82 jumps).

Play card 4, three roads for one number: the rabbit is at 8,327. Switch between the Tens, Hundreds and Thousands roads and choose the nearer carrot on each. Answer: tens 8,330 (3 jumps), hundreds 8,300 (27 jumps), thousands 8,000 (327 jumps).
Play card 5, one carrot for two numbers: place the rabbit at 6,298 and then at 6,303 on the Tens road. Answer: both go to 6,300 (2 jumps and 3 jumps), so they have the same nearest ten.

Challenge card 1: The rabbit is at 2,346. Its food has been kept at its neighbouring tens. On which tens should the rabbit go to get its food, with the least number of steps? Then do the same for the neighbouring hundreds and the neighbouring thousands: ___ is the nearest ten (hundred, thousand) of 2,346. It will need ___ jumps to reach ___. Answer: 2,350 with 4 jumps; 2,300 with 46 jumps; 2,000 with 346 jumps.

Challenge card 2: Fill in the boxes appropriately: the nearest tens, nearest hundreds and nearest thousands of 3,176, 4,017, 5,789 and 8,203. Answer: 3,176: 3,180; 3,200; 3,000. 4,017: 4,020; 4,000; 4,000. 5,789: 5,790; 5,800; 6,000. 8,203: 8,200; 8,200; 8,000.

A carrot that needs more jumps shows both counts with 'This carrot needs more jumps. Which carrot needs fewer?', and the rabbit stays so the student can try again.
A rabbit placed on a different number from the one on the card slides back with 'The rabbit is at ___. The card asks for ___.'
A correct choice makes the rabbit hop the jumps one by one with a gentle count, and the nearest number is written on the milestone.

On the three-roads card the road changes after each correct choice and a small row keeps the nearest ten, hundred and thousand found so far, so the student can see that the nearest mark can be below or above the number.
In the table, a box that is not right shows the two neighbours and the jumps to each, so the student can correct it.

media.title: The nearest ten
media.context: We the Travellers - I. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Explain the nearest ten with the neighbouring marks on a number line. It works this example: A rabbit is at 4,197. Its food is kept at the neighbouring tens. Which ten is nearest, and how many jumps does the rabbit need?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a rabbit sits at 4,197. Its food is kept at the two neighbouring tens. Which food will it jump to? The neighbouring tens are the ten just below and the ten just above. For 4,197 they are 4,190 and 4,200. Count the jumps. From 4,197 to 4,200 is 3 jumps. From 4,197 to 4,190 is 7 jumps. Fewer jumps means nearer. The picture also marks the halfway point of the road, 4,195. The rabbit at 4,197 stands on the 4,200 side of it. If the rabbit stood at 4,192, it would be on the 4,190 side. It would need 2 jumps to 4,190 and 8 jumps to 4,200, so it would go down. The nearest ten can be below or above. Do not pick the food that looks most like the number. 4,190 shares more digits with 4,197, but 4,200 is nearer. Rule: the nearest ten is the neighbouring ten with fewer jumps. 1. The neighbouring tens of 4,197 are 4,190 and 4,200. 2. Jumps to 4,200: 4,200 − 4,197 = 3. 3. Jumps to 4,190: 4,197 − 4,190 = 7. 4. 3 is less than 7, so 4,200 is nearer. The rabbit stands to the right of the halfway point 4,195, on the 4,200 side. 5. Check: 3 + 7 = 10, the gap between 4,190 and 4,200. Answer: 4,200 is the nearest ten of 4,197. The rabbit needs 3 jumps.

media.title: The nearest hundred and the nearest thousand
media.context: We the Travellers - I. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Explain the nearest hundred and the nearest thousand with neighbouring marks on a number line. It works this example: A rabbit is at 6,731. Find its nearest hundred and its nearest thousand, with the jumps.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a rabbit is at 6,731. Will it go to the same side for the hundreds line and for the thousands line? On the hundreds line the foods are at 6,700 and 6,800. It is 6,731 − 6,700 = 31 jumps to 6,700 and 6,800 − 6,731 = 69 jumps to 6,800. On the thousands line the foods are at 6,000 and 7,000. It is 6,731 − 6,000 = 731 jumps to 6,000 and 7,000 − 6,731 = 269 jumps to 7,000. So the nearest hundred of 6,731 is 6,700, below it, and the nearest thousand is 7,000, above it. Each line has its own two neighbours. Rule: choose the line, find the two neighbours, count the jumps to each and choose the fewer. 1. Hundreds: the neighbours of 6,731 are 6,700 and 6,800. 2. 6,731 − 6,700 = 31 jumps and 6,800 − 6,731 = 69 jumps. 31 is less than 69, so the nearest hundred is 6,700. 3. Thousands: the neighbours of 6,731 are 6,000 and 7,000. 4. 6,731 − 6,000 = 731 jumps and 7,000 − 6,731 = 269 jumps. 269 is less than 731, so the nearest thousand is 7,000. 5. Check: 31 + 69 = 100 and 731 + 269 = 1,000, the gaps between the neighbours. Answer: The nearest hundred of 6,731 is 6,700 (31 jumps) and the nearest thousand is 7,000 (269 jumps)

media.title: Numbers with the same nearest number
media.context: We the Travellers - I. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Students write two numbers that have the same nearest ten, hundred or thousand, and check their choice by counting the jumps of each number to both neighbours. It works this example: (a) Write two numbers that have the same nearest hundred. (b) Write two numbers that have the same nearest ten, nearest hundred and nearest thousand.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: can two different numbers have the same nearest hundred? Think of the rabbit and its food. Yes. Each food has numbers on both sides of it that are nearer to it than to any other food. Those numbers share the same nearest number. A number very close to a thousand, such as 8,000, is also close to the nearest hundred and the nearest ten, which are the same 8,000. To check two numbers, count the jumps of each to both of its neighbours on that line. Rule: two numbers have the same nearest number when both are nearer to the same food on that line. 1. (a) Pick the hundred 5,400 and take one number below it and one above it: 5,380 and 5,420. 2. 5,380 needs 5,400 − 5,380 = 20 jumps to 5,400 and 5,380 − 5,300 = 80 jumps to 5,300. 5,420 needs 5,420 − 5,400 = 20 jumps to 5,400 and 5,500 − 5,420 = 80 jumps to 5,500. Both have the nearest hundred 5,400. 3. (b) Pick the thousand 8,000 and take two numbers very close to it: 7,997 and 8,002. 4. Nearest ten: 7,997 needs 3 jumps to 8,000 and 7,997 − 7,990 = 7 jumps to 7,990. 8,002 needs 2 jumps to 8,000 and 8,010 − 8,002 = 8 jumps to 8,010. Both give 8,000. 5. Nearest hundred: 7,997 needs 3 jumps to 8,000 and 7,997 − 7,900 = 97 jumps to 7,900. 8,002 needs 2 jumps to 8,000 and 8,100 − 8,002 = 98 jumps to 8,100. Both give 8,000. 6. Nearest thousand: 7,997 needs 3 jumps to 8,000 and 7,997 − 7,000 = 997 jumps to 7,000. 8,002 needs 2 jumps to 8,000 and 9,000 − 8,002 = 998 jumps to 9,000. Both give 8,000. Answer: (a) 5,380 and 5,420, nearest hundred 5,400. (b) 7,997 and 8,002, nearest ten, nearest hundred and nearest thousand all 8,000.

concepts.concept_name: Nearest Numbers (rabbit), the neighbouring tens

content.text:
Nearest Numbers (rabbit), the neighbouring tens: A rabbit is hungry. The rabbit is at 2,346. Its food has been kept at its neighbouring tens, 2,340 and 2,350. On which tens should the rabbit go to get its food, with the least number of steps?
1. The neighbouring tens of 2,346 are 2,340 and 2,350.
2. Jumps to 2,350: 2,350 − 2,346 = 4.
3. Jumps to 2,340: 2,346 − 2,340 = 6.
4. 4 is less than 6, so 2,350 is nearer.
5. Check: 4 + 6 = 10, the gap between 2,340 and 2,350, and the rabbit stands just to the right of the halfway mark 2,345.
Answer: 2,350 is the nearest ten of 2,346. It will need 4 jumps to reach 2,350.

content.text:
Nearest Numbers (rabbit), the neighbouring hundreds: The rabbit is at 2,346. Its food has been kept at its neighbouring hundreds, 2,300 and 2,400. Which of the two hundreds should the rabbit go to? ___ is the nearest hundred of 2,346. It will need ___ jumps to reach ___.
1. The neighbouring hundreds of 2,346 are 2,300 and 2,400.
2. Jumps to 2,300: 2,346 − 2,300 = 46.
3. Jumps to 2,400: 2,400 − 2,346 = 54.
4. 46 is less than 54, so 2,300 is nearer.

Answer: 2,300 is the nearest hundred of 2,346. It will need 46 jumps to reach 2,300.

concepts.concept_name: Nearest Numbers (table), tens, hundreds and thousands

content.text:
Nearest Numbers (table), tens, hundreds and thousands: Fill in the boxes appropriately. Find the nearest tens, nearest hundreds and nearest thousands of 3,176, 4,017, 5,789 and 8,203.
1. 3,176, tens: 3,176 − 3,170 = 6 jumps and 3,180 − 3,176 = 4 jumps, so 3,180.
2. 3,176, hundreds: 76 jumps to 3,100 and 24 jumps to 3,200, so 3,200. Thousands: 176 jumps to 3,000 and 824 jumps to 4,000, so 3,000.
3. 4,017, tens: 7 jumps to 4,010 and 3 jumps to 4,020, so 4,020. Hundreds: 17 jumps to 4,000 and 83 jumps to 4,100, so 4,000. Thousands: 17 jumps to 4,000 and 983 jumps to 5,000, so 4,000.

concepts.concept_name: Let Us Think (nearest numbers), Q1 Vijay and Suma

content.text:
Let Us Think (nearest numbers), Q1 Vijay and Suma: Vijay rounded off a number to the nearest hundred. Suma rounded off the same number to the nearest thousand. Both got the same result. Circle the numbers they might have used. 7,126, 7,835, 7,030, 6,999.
1. Find the nearest hundred and the nearest thousand of each number.
2. 7,126: 26 jumps to 7,100 and 74 jumps to 7,200, so 7,100. 126 jumps to 7,000 and 874 jumps to 8,000, so 7,000. The results are different.
3. 7,835: 35 jumps to 7,800 and 65 jumps to 7,900, so 7,800. 835 jumps to 7,000 and 165 jumps to 8,000, so 8,000. The results are different.
4. 7,030: 30 jumps to 7,000 and 70 jumps to 7,100, so 7,000. 30 jumps to 7,000 and 970 jumps to 8,000, so 7,000. The results are the same.
5. 6,999: 99 jumps to 6,900 and 1 jump to 7,000, so 7,000. 999 jumps to 6,000 and 1 jump to 7,000, so 7,000. The results are the same.
6. Check: 7,030 is 30 above 7,000 and 6,999 is 1 below 7,000, so both stand right next to 7,000.
Answer: 7,030 and 6,999 (both give 7,000)

concepts.concept_name: Let Us Think (nearest numbers), Q2 same nearest ten, hundred, thousand

content.text:
Let Us Think (nearest numbers), Q2 same nearest ten, hundred, thousand: Think and write two numbers that have the same (a) Nearest ten. (b) Nearest hundred. (c) Nearest thousand. For example, 19 and 21 have the same nearest ten, that is, 20.
1. (a) Pick the ten 3,140. 3,138 is 2 jumps below it and 3,142 is 2 jumps above it.
2. The other tens are far: 3,138 − 3,130 = 8 jumps and 3,150 − 3,142 = 8 jumps. Both have the nearest ten 3,140.
3. (b) Pick the hundred 4,500. 4,480 is 20 jumps below it and 4,520 is 20 jumps above it.
4. The other hundreds are far: 4,480 − 4,400 = 80 jumps and 4,600 − 4,520 = 80 jumps. Both have the nearest hundred 4,500.
5. (c) Pick the thousand 6,000. 5,900 is 100 jumps below it and 6,200 is 200 jumps above it.
6. The other thousands are far: 5,900 − 5,000 = 900 jumps and 7,000 − 6,200 = 800 jumps. Both have the nearest thousand 6,000.
7. Check: 3,138 and 3,142 are both 2 from 3,140, 4,480 and 4,520 are both 20 from 4,500, and 5,900 and 6,200 are much nearer to 6,000 than to 5,000 or 7,000.
Answer: Sample answer: (a) 3,138 and 3,142; (b) 4,480 and 4,520; (c) 5,900 and 6,200. Your answer may differ.

concepts.concept_name: Let Us Think (nearest numbers), Q3 same in two or three places

content.text:
Let Us Think (nearest numbers), Q3 same in two or three places: Think and write the numbers that have the same (a) Nearest ten and nearest hundred. (b) Nearest hundred and nearest thousand. (c) Nearest ten, hundred and thousand.
1. (a) Pick the hundred 5,300 and numbers right next to it: 5,297 is 3 jumps below it and 5,302 is 2 jumps above it.
2. Their nearest ten is also 5,300: 5,297 is 7 jumps from 5,290 and 5,302 is 8 jumps from 5,310. Both give 5,300 for the ten and for the hundred.
3. (b) Pick the thousand 8,000. 7,970 is 30 jumps below it and 8,030 is 30 jumps above it. The other thousands are 970 jumps away, so both give 8,000.
4. Their nearest hundred is also 8,000: 7,970 is 70 jumps from 7,900 and 8,030 is 70 jumps from 8,100.
5. (c) Pick 4,000 and numbers very close to it: 3,998 is 2 jumps below it and 4,003 is 3 jumps above it.
6. The other tens are 3,998 − 3,990 = 8 and 4,010 − 4,003 = 7 jumps away. The other hundreds are 3,998 − 3,900 = 98 and 4,100 − 4,003 = 97 jumps away. The other thousands are 3,998 − 3,000 = 998 and 5,000 − 4,003 = 997 jumps away.
7. So 3,998 and 4,003 both have the nearest ten, hundred and thousand 4,000.
8. Check: 5,297 and 5,302 are within 3 of 5,300, 7,970 and 8,030 are 30 from 8,000, and 3,998 and 4,003 are within 3 of 4,000, far less than the jumps to the other marks.
Answer: Sample answer: (a) 5,297 and 5,302; (b) 7,970 and 8,030; (c) 3,998 and 4,003. Your answer may differ.

media.teaching_notes: 1. (a) Pick the hundred 5,300 and numbers right next to it: 5,297 is 3 jumps below it and 5,302 is 2 jumps above it. 2. So 3,998 and 4,003 both have the nearest ten, hundred and thousand 4,000. 8. Check: 5,297 and 5,302 are within 3 of 5,300, 7,970 and 8,030 are 30 from 8,000, and 3,998 and 4,003 are within 3 of 4,000, far less than the jumps to the other marks. modules.module_name: Large Numbers on the Move and Pastime Mathematics
modules.module_summary: How far vehicles travel in an hour and how many carry a school, large counts around us, three puzzles on a train, the King's Horses, and a revision of the whole journey.

segments.summary: People travelled on foot, on animals and in boats long ago, and now they use cycles, cars, trains, ships, aeroplanes and spacecraft. The book gives how far a person generally travels in one hour, from a 1-digit number to a 5-digit number of kilometres. The distance in many hours is the distance in one hour times the number of hours, and the vehicles needed for a group are the people divided by the people in one vehicle.

concepts.concept_name: Travelling, Now and Then

content.text:
We learnt that people in the past travelled on foot, on animals, and used boats and sailing ships. The animals that have been used for travelling include bullocks, horses, donkeys, mules, and elephants. In hilly and snow-covered regions, yaks, dogs, and reindeers have been used, while camels have been used in deserts.
Now, people use bicycles, motorbikes, cars, buses, trains, ships, and aeroplanes to travel from one place to another. Submarines are used to go deep under water. Humans are also using spacecraft to travel to outer space.

concepts.concept_name: How far in one hour?

content.text:
In an hour a person can generally travel
(a) 3 to 5 km on foot.
(b) 10 to 15 km on horseback.
(c) 12 to 20 km by cycle.
(d) 40 to 60 km by motorbike.
(e) 40 to 160 km by train.
(f) 25 to 45 km by ship.
(g) 750 to 920 km by aircraft.
(h) minimum 28,000 km by spacecraft.
Usually, we measure distances in sea and air using nautical miles. For now, we will use 1 km = 1,000 m. By now, you know different units of measuring length. We will study the units for measuring length, kilometre, in detail in a later chapter.

content.text:
Worked example: Suppose a traveller covers 50 km in one hour. Which means of travel in the book's list can do that, and how many digits does 50 have?
1. A means fits when 50 is at least its first number and at most its last number.
2. On foot (3 to 5), on horseback (10 to 15), by cycle (12 to 20) and by ship (25 to 45): 50 is more than the last number each time, so none fits.
3. By aircraft (750 to 920) and by spacecraft (minimum 28,000): 50 is less than the first number, so neither fits.
4. By motorbike (40 to 60): 40 is less than 50 and 50 is less than 60, so it fits.
5. By train (40 to 160): 40 is less than 50 and 50 is less than 160, so it fits.
6. 50 has 2 digits.
Answer: A motorbike or a train; 50 is a 2-digit number

concepts.concept_name: How many vehicles for a group?

content.text:
1. Predict first: 12 children go on a trip in cars that carry 4 children each. How many cars do they need, 3, 4 or 8?
2. Each car takes 4 children. Count in 4s: 4, 8, 12. That is 3 cars, and 12 ÷ 4 = 3.
3. The number of vehicles is the number of people divided by the number of people in one vehicle.
4. A vehicle that carries more people needs fewer vehicles. The same 12 children need 3 cars of 4, but only 2 big cars of 6, because 12 ÷ 6 = 2.
5. Check by multiplying: 3 × 4 = 12 and 2 × 6 = 12.
6. Rule: divide the people by the number one vehicle carries, then check by multiplying.

content.text:
Worked example: A group of 120 people goes on a trip. How many vehicles are needed if each car carries 4 people? How many if each big car carries 6 people?
1. People in the group: 120. People in one car: 4.
2. Cars needed: 120 ÷ 4 = 30.
3. Check: 30 × 4 = 120, so 30 cars carry all 120 people.
4. People in one big car: 6. Big cars needed: 120 ÷ 6 = 20.
5. Check: 20 × 6 = 120, so 20 big cars carry all 120 people.
6. A big car carries more people, so fewer vehicles are needed.
Answer: 30 cars, or 20 big cars
