tool_config.idea: Read the book's own numbers for travel and use them: how far a means of travel goes in one hour (from 3 to 5 km on foot to at least 28,000 km by spacecraft), how many digits that distance has, how far it goes in several hours (the distance in one hour times the hours), and how many vehicles a group needs (the people divided by the people one vehicle carries).
tool_config.screen: One clean, warm, colourful route map in a polished educational-game look: a 3D isometric landscape with soft shadows, clear shapes and gentle animation, where a winding route runs from a Start flag to a Finish flag across fields, a river bank and a sea shore. Nothing else is drawn: no crowds, no shops, no decoration off the route. The largest element is the distance card in the middle of the screen, with its numbers in very large type. A row of eight large vehicle buttons runs along the bottom, each with a picture and a name: Foot, Horseback, Cycle, Motorbike, Train, Ship, Aircraft, Spacecraft. Every control and read-out: (1) the eight vehicle buttons, one selected at a time; choosing one moves that vehicle a short way along the route. (2) The distance card, for example 'In 1 hour: 40 to 60 km', and for the spacecraft 'In 1 hour: at least 28,000 km'. (3) Digit chips under the card, one for each number on it, such as '2 digits', with the digits coloured by place. (4) An Hours stepper with minus and plus buttons from 1 to 4 hours and a Go button: the vehicle hops along the route once for each hour, every hop the same length, and a working line shows each end of the range times the hours, for example '10 × 3 = 30'. The label 'same distance every hour (practice)' sits beside it. The Hours stepper is greyed out for the spacecraft because the book gives only a minimum. (5) A group panel: a crowd drawn in groups of ten, a 'People' read-out, the 'People in one vehicle' read-out taken from the book's list (bicycle 2, autorickshaw 3, car 4, big car 6, tempo traveller 10, boat 20, minibus 25, aeroplane 180), a Load button that fills one vehicle at a time, a 'Vehicles used' counter and a 'People left' counter. (6) An answer box that opens on a challenge card, with a Check button. (7) Hint, Undo and Reset buttons, a progress strip of dots with one dot for each card, Back and Next buttons in the same bottom corners on every card, and a Restart button. Only the controls the current card needs are shown.
student_does: Phase 1, Recall and get ready: a cycle, a train and a spacecraft wait at the Start flag. Tap each one and read its card: the distance in one hour and how many digits it has.

Phase 2, Play and apply: tap a vehicle and read its card, find the means whose card holds a given distance, set the hours and watch the vehicle hop the same distance each hour while the card shows the multiplication, and load a group of people into one kind of vehicle to count the vehicles.

Phase 3, Challenge: the book's own questions, unchanged: the cyclist who covers 15 km in one hour (how far in 4 hours), and the school of 461 girls and 439 boys with the eight vehicles from the bicycle (2) to the aeroplane (180).
challenges: Card 1 (Phase 2, read): Tap Foot, then Spacecraft. How many digits does the number on each card have? Answer: foot, 3 to 5 km, 1 digit; spacecraft, at least 28,000 km, 5 digits.

Card 2 (Phase 2, find the means): Practice value: a traveller covers 30 km in one hour. Tap the vehicles and find the one whose card holds 30. Answer: the ship, 25 to 45 km, because 25 is less than 30 and 30 is less than 45; every other card misses 30.
Card 3 (Phase 2, hours): Pick Horseback and set 3 hours. Fill in both ends of the range for 3 hours, with the same distance every hour (practice). Answer: 10 × 3 = 30 and 15 × 3 = 45, so 30 to 45 km.

Card 4 (Phase 2, vehicles): Practice value: a group of 120 people. Load them into boats (20 each) and then into tempo travellers (10 each). How many of each, and which needs fewer? Answer: 120 ÷ 20 = 6 boats and 120 ÷ 10 = 12 tempo travellers; the boat carries more people, so fewer boats are needed.

Card 5 (Phase 3, the book's question): A cyclist can cover 15 km in one hour. How much distance will she cover in 4 hours, if she maintains the same speed? Answer: 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 = 60, so 15 × 4 = 60 km.

Card 6 (Phase 3, the book's question): A school has 461 girls and 439 boys. How many vehicles are needed for all of them to go on a trip using the following modes of travel? The numbers in the bracket indicate the number of people that can travel in one vehicle. (a) Bicycle (2) (b) Autorickshaw (3) (c) Car (4) (d) Big car (6) (e) Tempo traveller (10) (f) Boat (20) (g) Minibus (25) (h) Aeroplane (180). Answer: 461 + 439 = 900 people; 450, 300, 225, 150, 90, 45, 36 and 5 vehicles.
feedback: A right answer turns the card green with a tick, and the vehicle drives to the Finish flag. The working appears in one line, for example 10 × 3 = 30.
A distance that is not in the chosen range shows the range beside it and says whether the distance is less than the first number or more than the last number.
A wrong number of digits lights up the digits of the number one by one and counts them aloud.
A wrong number of hours or vehicles shows the hops or the loaded vehicles on the route and the people still left, so the student sees what is missing.
Each hour of the journey stays on the route as a hop of the same length, so the total is seen being built.
tool_config.done_when: Every card is done and the student has opened at least five of the eight vehicle cards.

media.title: How many vehicles for a group?
media.context: We the Travellers - I. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Students find the number of vehicles needed for a group by dividing the number of people by the number of people one vehicle carries, and check the answer by multiplying. It works this example: A group of 120 people goes on a trip. How many vehicles are needed if each car carries 4 people? How many if each big car carries 6 people?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: 12 children go on a trip in cars that carry 4 children each. How many cars do they need, 3, 4 or 8? Each car takes 4 children. Count in 4s: 4, 8, 12. That is 3 cars, and 12 ÷ 4 = 3. The number of vehicles is the number of people divided by the number of people in one vehicle. A vehicle that carries more people needs fewer vehicles. The same 12 children need 3 cars of 4, but only 2 big cars of 6, because 12 ÷ 6 = 2. Check by multiplying: 3 × 4 = 12 and 2 × 6 = 12. Rule: divide the people by the number one vehicle carries, then check by multiplying. 1. People in the group: 120. People in one car: 4. 2. Cars needed: 120 ÷ 4 = 30. 3. Check: 30 × 4 = 120, so 30 cars carry all 120 people. 4. People in one big car: 6. Big cars needed: 120 ÷ 6 = 20. 5. Check: 20 × 6 = 120, so 20 big cars carry all 120 people. 6. A big car carries more people, so fewer vehicles are needed. Answer: 30 cars, or 20 big cars

concepts.concept_name: Let Us Do (travelling), Q1 cyclist

content.text:
Let Us Do (travelling), Q1 cyclist: A cyclist can cover 15 km in one hour. How much distance will she cover in 4 hours, if she maintains the same speed?
1. In 1 hour the cyclist covers 15 km.
2. In 2 hours: 15 + 15 = 30 km.
3. In 3 hours: 30 + 15 = 45 km.
4. In 4 hours: 45 + 15 = 60 km.
5. Check by multiplying: 15 × 4 = 60 km.
Answer: 60 km

concepts.concept_name: Let Us Do (travelling), Q2 (a) to (d) vehicles

content.text:
Let Us Do (travelling), Q2 (a) to (d) vehicles: A school has 461 girls and 439 boys. How many vehicles are needed for all of them to go on a trip using the following modes of travel? The numbers in the bracket indicate the number of people that can travel in one vehicle. (a) Bicycle (2) (b) Autorickshaw (3) (c) Car (4) (d) Big car (6)
1. Add the girls and the boys: 461 + 439 = 900 people.
2. Vehicles needed = 900 ÷ the number of people in one vehicle.
3. (a) Bicycle: 900 ÷ 2 = 450.
4. (b) Autorickshaw: 900 ÷ 3 = 300.
5. (c) Car: 900 ÷ 4 = 225.
6. (d) Big car: 900 ÷ 6 = 150.
7. Check: 450 × 2 = 900, 300 × 3 = 900, 225 × 4 = 900 and 150 × 6 = 900.
Answer: (a) 450 (b) 300 (c) 225 (d) 150

3. (f) Boat: 900 ÷ 20 = 45.

5. (h) Aeroplane: 900 ÷ 180 = 5.
6. Check: 90 × 10 = 900, 45 × 20 = 900, 36 × 25 = 900 and 5 × 180 = 900.
Answer: (e) 90 (f) 45 (g) 36 (h) 5

concepts.concept_name: Where do large numbers hide?

content.text:
We saw that the distance (in kilometre) covered by different means of transport in an hour can range from a 1-digit number to a 5-digit number. Can we find other contexts around us that contain numbers in this range? Let us consider the situation below.
Now, let us try this with our school.
(a) Our school has ________ classrooms.
(b) There are ________ students in my class.
(c) Our classroom has ________ books in total.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a box holds 40 sheets of stickers and each sheet has 100 stickers. Will the number of stickers have 3 digits, 4 digits or 5 digits?
2. The distances in an hour that we met run from a 1-digit number, 3 km on foot, to a 5-digit number, at least 28,000 km by spacecraft. Large numbers hide in many other places too.
3. Count one small part, then multiply by the number of parts. The stickers are 100 × 40 = 4,000, a 4-digit number.
4. Now try it with your school: our school has ___ classrooms, there are ___ students in my class, and our classroom has ___ books in total. Say how many digits each count has.
5. Rule: count one small part, multiply by the number of parts, then count the digits.

content.text:
Worked example: Suppose each sheet has 100 stickers and a box holds 40 sheets. How many stickers are in the box? Is the count a 4-digit or a 5-digit number?
1. One sheet has 100 stickers.
2. 10 sheets have 100 × 10 = 1,000 stickers.
3. 40 sheets are 4 groups of 10 sheets: 4 × 1,000 = 4,000 stickers.
4. Check: 100 × 40 = 4,000.
5. 4,000 has 4 digits, so the count is a 4-digit number.
Answer: 4,000 stickers, a 4-digit number

concepts.concept_name: Finding Large Numbers Around Us, Example (words in a book)

content.text:
Finding Large Numbers Around Us, Example (words in a book): A book has around 200 pages, and each page has about 50 words. About how many words does the book have in all?
1. The book has about 200 pages.
2. Each page has about 50 words.
3. 100 pages have 100 × 50 = 5,000 words.
4. 200 pages are 2 times as many: 5,000 × 2 = 10,000 words.
5. Check: 200 × 50 = 10,000, and 10,000 has 5 digits.
Answer: About 10,000 words, a 5-digit number

concepts.concept_name: Finding Large Numbers Around Us, Try It (maths book)

content.text:
Finding Large Numbers Around Us, Try It (maths book): Find something in the maths book whose count is a 4-digit number.
1. Pick a thing to count: the words in one chapter of the maths book.
2. Estimate one part: a page has about 150 words.
3. Count the parts: the chapter has about 16 pages.
4. 10 pages have 10 × 150 = 1,500 words.
5. 6 pages have 6 × 150 = 900 words.
6. Add the parts: 1,500 + 900 = 2,400 words.
7. Check: 2,400 has 4 digits, so it is a 4-digit number.
Answer: Sample answer: the words in one chapter, about 2,400 (16 pages with about 150 words each), a 4-digit number. Your answer may differ.

concepts.concept_name: Finding Large Numbers Around Us, Try It (classroom)

content.text:
Finding Large Numbers Around Us, Try It (classroom): Find something in the classroom whose count is a (i) 4-digit number (ii) 5-digit number.
1. (i) Count the pages in one notebook from each child. Suppose the class has 40 children and a notebook has about 100 pages.
2. 10 notebooks have 10 × 100 = 1,000 pages.
3. 40 notebooks are 4 groups of 10: 4 × 1,000 = 4,000 pages, a 4-digit number.
4. (ii) Count all the notebooks. Suppose each child has 5 notebooks: 40 × 5 = 200 notebooks.
5. 200 notebooks with about 100 pages each: 200 × 100 = 20,000 pages, a 5-digit number.
6. Check the digits: 4,000 has 4 digits and 20,000 has 5 digits.
Answer: Sample answer: (i) pages in 40 notebooks, about 4,000, a 4-digit number; (ii) pages in 200 notebooks, about 20,000, a 5-digit number. Your answer may differ.

concepts.concept_name: Finding Large Numbers Around Us, Try It (tree, village or town)

content.text:
Finding Large Numbers Around Us, Try It (tree, village or town): List some quantities whose count is a 4-digit or a 5-digit number in the context of (i) a tree (ii) your village/town/city, or any other place of your choice.
1. (i) A tree: count the leaves. Suppose a twig has 30 leaves and the tree has 90 twigs.
2. 10 twigs have 30 × 10 = 300 leaves.
3. 90 twigs are 9 groups of 10 twigs: 300 × 9 = 2,700 leaves, a 4-digit number.
4. A garden of 10 such trees has 2,700 × 10 = 27,000 leaves, a 5-digit number.
5. (ii) A town: count the windows. Suppose a street has 50 houses and a house has 4 windows: 50 × 4 = 200 windows on a street.
6. 30 streets have 200 × 30 = 6,000 windows, a 4-digit number.
7. 100 streets have 200 × 100 = 20,000 windows, a 5-digit number.
8. Check the digits: 2,700 and 6,000 have 4 digits; 27,000 and 20,000 have 5 digits.
Answer: Sample answer: (i) leaves on a tree, about 2,700 (4-digit), and in a garden of 10 trees, about 27,000 (5-digit); (ii) windows in a town, about 6,000 (4-digit) or 20,000 (5-digit). Your answer may differ.

concepts.concept_name: River Crossing Puzzle

content.text:
Sanju and Mira are traveling on a train. To pass time, they challenge each other with games and puzzles.
Mira poses the river crossing puzzle to Sanju.
A boatman wants to cross a river in a boat. He has to take a lion, a sheep, and a bundle of grass with him. He can take one of them at a time. If the sheep and grass are left on the shore, the sheep will eat the grass. And, if the sheep and lion are left on the shore, the lion will eat the sheep.

Mira poses the river crossing puzzle to Sanju.

A boatman wants to cross a river in a boat. He has to take a lion, a sheep, and a bundle of grass with him. He can take one of them at a time. If the sheep and grass are left on the shore, the sheep will eat the grass. And, if the sheep and lion are left on the shore, the lion will eat the sheep.

content.text:
1. Predict first: the boatman takes one thing at a time. Which one should he take first, so that nothing is eaten?
2. Sanju and Mira use puzzles to pass the time on the train. A puzzle is solved by thinking, step by step, and puzzles like this train us to think logically and strategically.
3. Start with the rules. Whatever the boatman takes across, the other two stay behind, so list the pairs that could be left alone.
4. The lion and the sheep cannot stay together, and the sheep and the grass cannot stay together. The lion and the grass can.
5. The sheep is in both pairs that cannot stay together, so it cannot be left behind with anything. The first crossing is forced.
6. Rule: before you move anything, list which pairs are safe to leave alone, because the safe pairs decide your moves.

content.text:
Worked example: The boatman has a lion, a sheep and a bundle of grass. Which pairs can he leave alone on a bank, and what does that tell us about his first crossing?
1. The boat takes one thing at a time, so every crossing leaves two things behind on the bank.
2. List the three pairs he could leave behind: lion and sheep, sheep and grass, lion and grass.
3. Lion and sheep: the lion eats the sheep, so this pair cannot be left alone.
4. Sheep and grass: the sheep eats the grass, so this pair cannot be left alone.
5. Lion and grass: nothing in the rules is eaten, so this pair can be left alone.
6. If he takes the lion first, the sheep and the grass are left behind. That is not allowed. If he takes the grass first, the lion and the sheep are left behind. That is not allowed either.
7. If he takes the sheep first, the lion and the grass are left behind, which is allowed. So the first crossing is forced: the sheep goes first.
Answer: Only the lion and the grass can be left alone, so the sheep must cross first

concepts.concept_name: Pile of Pebbles

content.text:
Sanju introduces a game called pile of pebbles to Mira.
There are two piles of pebbles. Each pile contains 7 pebbles. Each player can pick as many pebbles they want from either of the piles. The player who picks the last pebble wins.
Try this game with your friends. Now, how do you play so that you win?
To find a winning strategy, try playing with 1 pebble in each pile, two in each, three in each, and so on.

Try this game with your friends. Now, how do you play so that you win?
To find a winning strategy, try playing with 1 pebble in each pile, two in each, three in each, and so on.

content.text:
1. Predict first: two piles have 2 pebbles each, and you play second. Can you always win?
2. In one turn a player picks as many pebbles as they want from one pile. The player who picks the last pebble wins.
3. A big game is hard to see, so play the smallest game first. With 1 and 1, your friend takes 1 pebble and you take the last one.
4. Now play 2 and 2. Write every move your friend can make and your answer to it. In both cases you take the last pebble.
5. Rule: when a game is big, play the small game first, write every move, and look for what stays the same.

content.text:
Worked example: Two piles have 2 pebbles each. You play second. Write every first move your friend can make and your answer to it. Who wins, and what stays the same?
1. Start with 2 and 2. Your friend can take 2 pebbles from one pile, or take 1 pebble from one pile.
2. If your friend takes 2 from one pile, the piles are 0 and 2.
3. You take the 2 pebbles of the other pile. The piles are 0 and 0. You took the last pebble and win.
4. If your friend takes 1 from one pile, the piles are 1 and 2.
5. You take 1 from the pile of 2. The piles are 1 and 1.
6. Your friend must take 1 from a pile. The piles are 0 and 1.
7. You take the last pebble and win.
8. Look at the piles after each of your moves: 0 and 0, and 1 and 1. Both times the two piles were equal.
Answer: With 2 and 2 the player who goes second wins every game, and after each move of that player the two piles are equal

concepts.concept_name: Fun Puzzle: subtract and repeat

content.text:
Now, it's Mira's turn. She gives a fun puzzle to Sanju with the following steps:
(a) Take any two different digits.
(b) Make two 2-digit numbers using them.
(c) Subtract the smaller number from the bigger number.
Now, use the two digits in the difference and repeat steps (b) and (c).
Continue this process until you get a 1-digit number. Even before everyone could finish, Mira exclaimed, "Mind you! No matter which two numbers you choose, you will get 9 in the end."

content.text:
1. Predict first: take the digits 2 and 5 and follow Mira's steps. What do you think you will get at the end?
2. Step (a): the digits are 2 and 5. Step (b): the numbers are 25 and 52. Step (c): 52 − 25 = 27.
3. Repeat with the digits 2 and 7: 72 − 27 = 45. Repeat with 4 and 5: 54 − 45 = 9. We stop at a 1-digit number.
4. Write every step in a row and look for what is common. The differences 27, 45 and 9 are all in the table of 9.
5. Do not mix up two differences. The digits 2 and 5 differ by 3, but the numbers 25 and 52 differ by 27.
6. Rule: when a puzzle repeats a step, write down every round and look for what stays the same.

content.text:
Worked example: Follow Mira's steps with the digits 2 and 5. What do you get at the end, and what do you notice about the differences?
1. Take the digits 2 and 5. The two 2-digit numbers are 25 and 52.
2. Subtract the smaller from the bigger: 52 − 25 = 27.
3. Use the two digits of 27, which are 2 and 7. The numbers are 27 and 72, and 72 − 27 = 45.
4. Use the two digits of 45, which are 4 and 5. The numbers are 45 and 54, and 54 − 45 = 9.
5. 9 has one digit, so we stop. The end is 9.
6. Look at the differences 27, 45 and 9. They are all in the table of 9: 27 = 9 × 3, 45 = 9 × 5 and 9 = 9 × 1.
7. The digits 2 and 5 differ by 3, because 5 − 2 = 3. The numbers 25 and 52 differ by 27. These are two different differences.
Answer: 52 − 25 = 27, 72 − 27 = 45, 54 − 45 = 9: the end is 9, and the differences are all in the table of 9

media.title: Puzzle Lab

tool_config.title: Puzzle Lab
tool_config.idea: Play the book's three pastime puzzles with their exact rules and find the thinking that wins each one: the safe pairs in the river, the equal piles in the pebbles game, and the table of 9 in Mira's digits.
tool_config.screen: A warm, colourful, polished educational-game scene: a compact hub on a small isometric table inside a train compartment, with three large door cards, River Crossing, Pile of Pebbles and Fun Puzzle (digits), soft shadows, gentle animation and no clutter. One door opens one scene at a time, and the puzzle board is always the largest thing on screen. River Crossing: a river with a near bank and a far bank, a boat for the boatman and one thing, and a large lion, sheep and bundle of grass that the student taps to put in the boat. Controls: Cross (the boat moves), Undo, Reset. Read-outs: a trip counter (Trips), the names of who is on each bank, and a Safe or Not safe banner for the bank the boatman has just left. Pile of Pebbles: two large piles of pebbles drawn as stacks, with a pile size choice of 1, 2, 3 or 7 pebbles in each pile (1, 2 and 3 are practice games, 7 is the book's game). The student taps pebbles on one pile to choose how many to take and the chosen pebbles lift. Controls: Take, Who plays first (You or Computer), Undo, Reset. The computer partner plays any allowed move. Read-outs: Your turn or Computer's turn, and the number of pebbles in each pile. Fun Puzzle (digits): two digit slots with tiles 1 to 9, and a rule note that the two digits must be different. Controls: Make numbers (shows the two 2-digit numbers), Subtract (shows the bigger number minus the smaller number and the difference), Use these digits (feeds the two digits of the difference into the slots for the next round), Undo, Reset. Read-outs: a growing list of every round, and a stamp when one digit is left. On every scene: Hint, Back and Next in the same place, progress dots and a Restart button.
student_does: Phase 1, Recall and get ready: each door card shows one small picture and one question from the videos, which pair can be left alone on a bank, what stays the same after the second player's move, and what is common in the differences. The student taps an answer to open the door.

Phase 2, Play and apply: the student moves the lion, sheep and grass into the boat and across the river and watches the Safe or Not safe banner, plays small piles of pebbles against the computer, and runs Mira's steps on digits of their own choice while reading each difference.

Phase 3, Challenge: the student solves each puzzle exactly as the book gives it: the river crossing with the lion, sheep and grass in the fewest trips, the two piles of 7 pebbles played so that they win, and Mira's process with the digits 3 and 7, then digits whose numbers differ by 27.
challenges: Phase 2, river: tick the pairs that can be left alone on a bank: lion and sheep, sheep and grass, lion and grass. Answer: only the lion and the grass.
Phase 2, river: make the first crossing so that nothing is eaten. Answer: take the sheep across, because the lion and the grass can stay together.

Phase 2, pebbles: choose 2 pebbles in each pile and let the computer play first. Whatever the computer takes from one pile, take the same number from the other pile. Answer: you take the last pebble and win.
Phase 2, digits: choose the digits 1 and 6, then press Make numbers, Subtract and Use these digits until one digit is left. Answer: 61 − 16 = 45, then 54 − 45 = 9.

Phase 3, river: How can the boatman take the lion, sheep, and grass across the river? Help him so that he can ferry the lion, sheep, and grass across the river safely, and in the minimum number of trips. Answer: 7 trips: take the sheep across, go back alone, take the lion across, bring the sheep back, take the grass across, go back alone, take the sheep across.

Phase 3, pebbles: There are two piles of pebbles. Each pile contains 7 pebbles. Each player can pick as many pebbles they want from either of the piles. The player who picks the last pebble wins. Try this game with your friends. Now, how do you play so that you win? Answer: let the other player go first, and whatever they take from one pile, take the same number from the other pile. You take the last pebble.

Phase 3, Mira's puzzle: take any two different digits, make two 2-digit numbers using them, subtract the smaller number from the bigger number, then use the two digits in the difference and repeat until you get a 1-digit number. Start with the digits 3 and 7. Then find different digits such that the difference between the numbers is 27. Answer: 73 − 37 = 36, 63 − 36 = 27, 72 − 27 = 45, 54 − 45 = 9. Digits that differ by 3 give 27, for example 1 and 4 with 41 − 14 = 27.

A move that tries to put two things in the boat is refused with the message that the boat takes one thing at a time.

media.title: River Crossing Puzzle
media.context: We the Travellers - I. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Present the river crossing puzzle, its objects and its rules exactly, and invite the student to think about a solution without changing the rules. It works this example: The boatman has a lion, a sheep and a bundle of grass. Which pairs can he leave alone on a bank, and what does that tell us about his first crossing?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: the boatman takes one thing at a time. Which one should he take first, so that nothing is eaten? Sanju and Mira use puzzles to pass the time on the train. A puzzle is solved by thinking, step by step, and puzzles like this train us to think logically and strategically. Start with the rules. Whatever the boatman takes across, the other two stay behind, so list the pairs that could be left alone. The lion and the sheep cannot stay together, and the sheep and the grass cannot stay together. The lion and the grass can. The sheep is in both pairs that cannot stay together, so it cannot be left behind with anything. The first crossing is forced. Rule: before you move anything, list which pairs are safe to leave alone, because the safe pairs decide your moves. 1. The boat takes one thing at a time, so every crossing leaves two things behind on the bank. 2. List the three pairs he could leave behind: lion and sheep, sheep and grass, lion and grass. 3. Lion and sheep: the lion eats the sheep, so this pair cannot be left alone. 4. Sheep and grass: the sheep eats the grass, so this pair cannot be left alone. 5. Lion and grass: nothing in the rules is eaten, so this pair can be left alone. 6. If he takes the lion first, the sheep and the grass are left behind. That is not allowed. If he takes the grass first, the lion and the sheep are left behind. That is not allowed either. 7. If he takes the sheep first, the lion and the grass are left behind, which is allowed. So the first crossing is forced: the sheep goes first. Answer: Only the lion and the grass can be left alone, so the sheep must cross first

media.title: Fun Puzzle: subtract and repeat

media.description: Concept video: Explain the number puzzle of Mira step by step with clear working. It works this example: Follow Mira's steps with the digits 2 and 5. What do you get at the end, and what do you notice about the differences?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: take the digits 2 and 5 and follow Mira's steps. What do you think you will get at the end? Step (a): the digits are 2 and 5. Step (b): the numbers are 25 and 52. Step (c): 52 − 25 = 27. Repeat with the digits 2 and 7: 72 − 27 = 45. Repeat with 4 and 5: 54 − 45 = 9. We stop at a 1-digit number. Write every step in a row and look for what is common. The differences 27, 45 and 9 are all in the table of 9. Do not mix up two differences. The digits 2 and 5 differ by 3, but the numbers 25 and 52 differ by 27. Rule: when a puzzle repeats a step, write down every round and look for what stays the same. 1. Take the digits 2 and 5. The two 2-digit numbers are 25 and 52. 2. Subtract the smaller from the bigger: 52 − 25 = 27. 3. Use the two digits of 27, which are 2 and 7. The numbers are 27 and 72, and 72 − 27 = 45. 4. Use the two digits of 45, which are 4 and 5. The numbers are 45 and 54, and 54 − 45 = 9. 5. 9 has one digit, so we stop. The end is 9. 6. Look at the differences 27, 45 and 9. They are all in the table of 9: 27 = 9 × 3, 45 = 9 × 5 and 9 = 9 × 1. 7. The digits 2 and 5 differ by 3, because 5 − 2 = 3. The numbers 25 and 52 differ by 27. These are two different differences. Answer: 52 − 25 = 27, 72 − 27 = 45, 54 − 45 = 9: the end is 9, and the differences are all in the table of 9

concepts.concept_name: Pastime Mathematics (river crossing), Q1

content.text:
Pastime Mathematics (river crossing), Q1: A boatman wants to cross a river in a boat. He has to take a lion, a sheep, and a bundle of grass with him. He can take one of them at a time. If the sheep and grass are left on the shore, the sheep will eat the grass. And, if the sheep and lion are left on the shore, the lion will eat the sheep. How can the boatman take the lion, sheep, and grass across the river? Help him so that he can ferry the lion, sheep, and grass across the river safely, and in the minimum number of trips.
1. Call the two banks the near bank and the far bank. At the start the lion, the sheep, the grass and the boatman are on the near bank.
2. The boat takes one thing at a time. Only the lion and the grass can be left alone together.
3. Trip 1: take the sheep across. The lion and the grass stay on the near bank, which is safe. The sheep is on the far bank.
4. Trip 2: go back alone. The sheep waits alone on the far bank.
5. Trip 3: take the lion across. The grass is alone on the near bank. The lion and the sheep are on the far bank with the boatman.
6. Trip 4: bring the sheep back. The lion waits alone on the far bank. The sheep and the grass are on the near bank with the boatman.
7. Trip 5: take the grass across. The sheep waits alone on the near bank. The lion and the grass are together on the far bank, which is safe.
8. Trip 6: go back alone. The lion and the grass stay together on the far bank, which is safe.
9. Trip 7: take the sheep across. The lion, the sheep and the grass are all on the far bank.
10. Count the trips: 4 trips to the far bank and 3 trips back, and 4 + 3 = 7 trips.
11. Fewer trips do not work. After the sheep and the lion are both across, going back alone would leave them together, so the sheep must come back once.
12. Check: in every trip the boatman left behind only the lion and the grass, or one thing alone. The sheep was never left with the lion or with the grass.
Answer: 7 trips: take the sheep across, go back alone, take the lion across, bring the sheep back, take the grass across, go back alone, take the sheep across

concepts.concept_name: Pastime Mathematics (pile of pebbles), Q2

content.text:
Pastime Mathematics (pile of pebbles), Q2: There are two piles of pebbles. Each pile contains 7 pebbles. Each player can pick as many pebbles they want from either of the piles. The player who picks the last pebble wins. Try this game with your friends. Now, how do you play so that you win? To find a winning strategy, try playing with 1 pebble in each pile, two in each, three in each, and so on.
1. Let your friend play first. You play second. In one turn a player takes pebbles from one pile.
2. The plan: whatever number of pebbles your friend takes from one pile, take the same number from the other pile.
3. Start with 7 and 7. Your friend takes 3 from the first pile: the piles are 4 and 7.
4. You take 3 from the second pile: the piles are 4 and 4.
5. Your friend takes 1 from the second pile: the piles are 4 and 3.
6. You take 1 from the first pile: the piles are 3 and 3.
7. Your friend takes 3 from the first pile: the piles are 0 and 3.
8. You take 3 from the second pile: the piles are 0 and 0. You took the last pebble and you win.
9. Why it works: after each of your moves the two piles are equal (4 and 4, 3 and 3, 0 and 0). Your friend takes from only one pile, so your friend can never empty both piles at once.
10. Check with small piles: with 1 and 1, your friend takes 1 and you take the last one. With 2 and 2 and with 3 and 3 the same copying wins.
Answer: Let your friend play first. Whatever your friend takes from one pile, take the same number from the other pile. The piles stay equal and you take the last pebble

To find a winning strategy, try playing with 1 pebble in each pile, two in each, three in each, and so on.
1. Let your friend play first. You play second. In one turn a player takes pebbles from one pile.
2. The plan: whatever number of pebbles your friend takes from one pile, take the same number from the other pile.
3. Start with 7 and 7. Your friend takes 3 from the first pile: the piles are 4 and 7.
4. You take 3 from the second pile: the piles are 4 and 4.
5. Your friend takes 1 from the second pile: the piles are 4 and 3.
6. You take 1 from the first pile: the piles are 3 and 3.
7. Your friend takes 3 from the first pile: the piles are 0 and 3.
8. You take 3 from the second pile: the piles are 0 and 0. You took the last pebble and you win.
9. Why it works: after each of your moves the two piles are equal (4 and 4, 3 and 3, 0 and 0). Your friend takes from only one pile, so your friend can never empty both piles at once.
10. Check with small piles: with 1 and 1, your friend takes 1 and you take the last one. With 2 and 2 and with 3 and 3 the same copying wins.
Answer: Let your friend play first. Whatever your friend takes from one pile, take the same number from the other pile. The piles stay equal and you take the last pebble

concepts.concept_name: Pastime Mathematics (Mira's puzzle), Q3 the process

content.text:
Pastime Mathematics (Mira's puzzle), Q3 the process: (a) Take any two different digits, for example 3 and 7. (b) Make two 2-digit numbers using them: 37 and 73. (c) Subtract the smaller number from the bigger number: 73 − 37 = 36. Now, use the two digits in the difference and repeat steps (b) and (c). Continue this process until you get a 1-digit number. Write the whole process.
1. Start with the digits 3 and 7. The numbers are 73 and 37, and 73 − 37 = 36.
2. Use the digits 3 and 6 of the difference. The numbers are 63 and 36.
3. 63 − 36 = 27.
4. Use the digits 2 and 7. The numbers are 72 and 27.
5. 72 − 27 = 45.
6. Use the digits 4 and 5. The numbers are 54 and 45.
7. 54 − 45 = 9.
8. 9 has one digit, so the process stops.
9. Check by adding back: 9 + 45 = 54, 45 + 27 = 72, 27 + 36 = 63 and 36 + 37 = 73.
Answer: 73 − 37 = 36, 63 − 36 = 27, 72 − 27 = 45, 54 − 45 = 9. The process ends in 9

concepts.concept_name: Pastime Mathematics (Mira's puzzle), Q3 explore (1) to (4)

content.text:
Pastime Mathematics (Mira's puzzle), Q3 explore (1) to (4): How did Mira know what the 1-digit number in the end would be? Let us explore. (1) Observe the differences you get in each step of the process for the digits 3 and 7: 36, 27, 45 and 9. Do you notice anything in common? (2) Try the puzzle using any other pair of digits. What is common to these differences? What do you get in the end? (3) What digits can you choose so that you get a 1-digit number in the first step itself? Give some examples. Describe the pattern in the digits. (4) Now, find different digits such that the difference between the numbers is 27.
1. (1) Look at the four differences: 36, 27, 45 and 9.
2. 36 = 9 × 4, 27 = 9 × 3, 45 = 9 × 5 and 9 = 9 × 1. All four are in the table of 9. That is what they have in common.
3. (2) Try the digits 4 and 9. The numbers are 49 and 94, and 94 − 49 = 45.
4. Use the digits 4 and 5. The numbers are 45 and 54, and 54 − 45 = 9.
5. The difference 45 is in the table of 9, and the end is 9 again.
6. (3) A 1-digit number in the first step needs a difference of 9. Try 21 − 12 = 9, 32 − 23 = 9 and 54 − 45 = 9.
7. In each pair the digits are next to each other, like 1 and 2, 2 and 3, 4 and 5. They differ by 1.
8. (4) Try the digits 1 and 4. The numbers are 14 and 41, and 41 − 14 = 27.
9. Other pairs that differ by 3 also work. The digits 2 and 5: 52 − 25 = 27. The digits 3 and 6: 63 − 36 = 27. The digits 4 and 7: 74 − 47 = 27. The digits 5 and 8: 85 − 58 = 27. The digits 6 and 9: 96 − 69 = 27.
10. Check: 41 − 14 = 27, and 4 − 1 = 3.
Answer: (1) all in the table of 9 (2) the digits 4 and 9 also end in 9, with differences in the table of 9 (3) digits next to each other, such as 4 and 5 (4) digits that differ by 3, such as 1 and 4

concepts.concept_name: Pastime Mathematics (Mira's puzzle), Q3 (5) the table

content.text:
Pastime Mathematics (Mira's puzzle), Q3 (5) the table: Mira found an interesting relationship between the two digits and the difference obtained. Can you see it in the table that Mira made? Digits 3, 7: 7 − 3 = 4 and 73 − 37 = 36. Digits 1, 9: 9 − 1 = 8 and 91 − 19 = 72. Digits 2, 8: 8 − 2 = 6 and 82 − 28 = 54. Digits 4, 5: 5 − 4 = 1 and 54 − 45 = 9. Extend this table by choosing appropriate digits so that the resulting differences are 2, 3, 5, and 7 respectively. What do the differences between the digits indicate?
1. Difference 2: choose the digits 1 and 3, because 3 − 1 = 2. Then 31 − 13 = 18.
2. Difference 3: choose the digits 1 and 4, because 4 − 1 = 3. Then 41 − 14 = 27.
3. Difference 5: choose the digits 1 and 6, because 6 − 1 = 5. Then 61 − 16 = 45.
4. Difference 7: choose the digits 1 and 8, because 8 − 1 = 7. Then 81 − 18 = 63.
5. Compare each digit difference with its number difference: 36 = 9 × 4, 72 = 9 × 8, 54 = 9 × 6 and 9 = 9 × 1.
6. The new rows agree: 18 = 9 × 2, 27 = 9 × 3, 45 = 9 × 5 and 63 = 9 × 7.
7. So the difference of the numbers is 9 times the difference of the digits.
8. Why: 73 has 4 more tens than 37, which is 40 more, but 4 fewer ones. So 40 − 4 = 36, and 36 = 9 × 4.
9. Check: the digits 4 and 5 differ by 1 and 54 − 45 = 9 = 9 × 1.
Answer: New rows: 1 and 3 give 18, 1 and 4 give 27, 1 and 6 give 45, 1 and 8 give 63. The difference of the numbers is 9 times the difference of the digits

concepts.concept_name: Pastime Mathematics (Mira's puzzle), Q3 three questions

content.text:
Pastime Mathematics (Mira's puzzle), Q3 three questions: List the numbers that give a 1-digit number in the third subtraction. Identify pairs of digits that lead to the 1-digit number after the maximum possible number of subtractions. Compare your answers with your friends.
1. Use the digits 1 to 9, so that both numbers have 2 digits. Count the subtractions for each gap between the digits.
2. Gap 1, such as 4 and 5: 54 − 45 = 9. That is 1 subtraction.
3. Gap 2, such as 1 and 3: 31 − 13 = 18, 81 − 18 = 63, 63 − 36 = 27, 72 − 27 = 45, 54 − 45 = 9. That is 5 subtractions.
4. Gap 3, such as 2 and 5: 52 − 25 = 27, 72 − 27 = 45, 54 − 45 = 9. That is 3 subtractions.
5. Gap 4, such as 3 and 7: 73 − 37 = 36, 63 − 36 = 27, 72 − 27 = 45, 54 − 45 = 9. That is 4 subtractions.
6. Gap 5, such as 1 and 6: 61 − 16 = 45, 54 − 45 = 9. That is 2 subtractions. Gap 6, such as 1 and 7: 71 − 17 = 54, 54 − 45 = 9. That is 2 subtractions.
7. Gap 7, such as 1 and 8: 81 − 18 = 63, 63 − 36 = 27, 72 − 27 = 45, 54 − 45 = 9. That is 4 subtractions.
8. Gap 8, such as 1 and 9: 91 − 19 = 72, 72 − 27 = 45, 54 − 45 = 9. That is 3 subtractions.
9. A 1-digit number comes in the third subtraction for gap 3 or gap 8. The pairs are 1 and 4, 2 and 5, 3 and 6, 4 and 7, 5 and 8, 6 and 9, and 1 and 9.
10. The numbers they make are 14 and 41, 25 and 52, 36 and 63, 47 and 74, 58 and 85, 69 and 96, and 19 and 91.
11. The most subtractions is 5, for gap 2. The pairs are 1 and 3, 2 and 4, 3 and 5, 4 and 6, 5 and 7, 6 and 8, 7 and 9.
12. Check with 2 and 4: 42 − 24 = 18, 81 − 18 = 63, 63 − 36 = 27, 72 − 27 = 45, 54 − 45 = 9. That is 5 subtractions.
Answer: Third subtraction: digits that differ by 3 (1 and 4, 2 and 5, 3 and 6, 4 and 7, 5 and 8, 6 and 9) or by 8 (1 and 9). Most subtractions, 5: digits that differ by 2 (1 and 3, 2 and 4, 3 and 5, 4 and 6, 5 and 7, 6 and 8, 7 and 9)

media.teaching_notes: 1. Call the two banks the near bank and the far bank. At the start the lion, the sheep, the grass and the boatman are on the near bank. 2. The boat takes one thing at a time. Only the lion and the grass can be left alone together. 3. Trip 1: take the sheep across. The lion and the grass stay on the near bank, which is safe. The sheep is on the far bank. 4. Trip 2: go back alone. The sheep waits alone on the far bank. 5. Trip 3: take the lion across. The grass is alone on the near bank. The lion and the sheep are on the far bank with the boatman. 6. Trip 4: bring the sheep back. The lion waits alone on the far bank. The sheep and the grass are on the near bank with the boatman. 7. Trip 5: take the grass across. The sheep waits alone on the near bank. The lion and the grass are together on the far bank, which is safe. 8. Trip 6: go back alone. The lion and the grass stay together on the far bank, which is safe. 9. Trip 7: take the sheep across. The lion, the sheep and the grass are all on the far bank. 10. Count the trips: 4 trips to the far bank and 3 trips back, and 4 + 3 = 7 trips. 11. Fewer trips do not work. After the sheep and the lion are both across, going back alone would leave them together, so the sheep must come back once. 12. Check: in every trip the boatman left behind only the lion and the grass, or one thing alone. The sheep was never left with the lion or with the grass. Answer: 7 trips: take the sheep across, go back alone, take the lion across, bring the sheep back, take the grass across, go back alone, take the sheep across

The difference 45 is in the table of 9, and the end is 9 again. 6. (3) A 1-digit number in the first step needs a difference of 9. Try 21 − 12 = 9, 32 − 23 = 9 and 54 − 45 = 9. 7. In each pair the digits are next to each other, like 1 and 2, 2 and 3, 4 and 5. They differ by 1. 8. (4) Try the digits 1 and 4. The numbers are 14 and 41, and 41 − 14 = 27. 9. Other pairs that differ by 3 also work. The digits 2 and 5: 52 − 25 = 27. The digits 3 and 6: 63 − 36 = 27. The digits 4 and 7: 74 − 47 = 27. The digits 5 and 8: 85 − 58 = 27. The digits 6 and 9: 96 − 69 = 27. 10. Check: 41 − 14 = 27, and 4 − 1 = 3. Answer: (1) all in the table of 9 (2) the digits 4 and 9 also end in 9, with differences in the table of 9 (3) digits next to each other, such as 4 and 5 (4) digits that differ by 3, such as 1 and 4

Check: the digits 4 and 5 differ by 1 and 54 − 45 = 9 = 9 × 1. Answer: New rows: 1 and 3 give 18, 1 and 4 give 27, 1 and 6 give 45, 1 and 8 give 63. concepts.concept_name: King's Horses: counting along the sides

content.text:
Once upon a time, there was a king who was very fond of horses. He had 20 horses of the best breed. The horses were kept in the royal stable, and cared for by a caretaker.
One night, a thief stole one of the horses. Fearing punishment, the caretaker arranged the horses in the stable as shown in the picture here.
The next day, when the king came to check on the horses, the caretaker led him around the square stable. "Please count the number of horses along each side, your majesty," he said.
The king counted 5 horses along each side. "We have 5 horses along each side and there are 4 sides. So there are a total of 20 horses, your majesty," the caretaker explained.
Satisfied with the explanation, the king returned to his palace.

content.text:
1. Predict first: 12 children stand around a square, 4 on each side, and the 4 corner children belong to two sides. Will 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 give the number of children?
2. 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16, which is more than 12. Each corner child was counted on two sides, once for each side.
3. There are 4 corners, so 4 children were counted twice. Take the extra counts away: 16 − 4 = 12.
4. Rule: counting along the sides counts every corner twice, so the real number is the total of the sides minus the corner ones counted twice.
5. Keep this rule in mind for the king's stable: a square stable has corners too.

content.text:
Worked example: 12 children stand around a square, 4 on each side, with one child at each corner. Sanju adds the four side counts. What does he get, and why is it not 12?
1. Each side has 4 children, counted from corner to corner.
2. Add the four sides: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16.
3. 16 is more than 12, so some children were counted twice.
4. A corner child stands on two sides, so that child is counted once for each side.
5. There are 4 corner children, each counted twice, so there are 4 extra counts.
6. Take the extra counts away: 16 − 4 = 12.
7. Check by counting each child once: 4 corner children, and 2 children between the corners on each side, 4 × 2 = 8. Then 4 + 8 = 12.
Answer: He gets 16, but there are only 12 children, because the 4 corner children are counted twice: 16 − 4 = 12

content.text:
A horse in a corner stall is counted on two sides.
The horses in the stable = 4 × 5 − the horses in the corner stalls.
Count the horses one by one to check the total.

tool_config.title: King's Horses Challenge
tool_config.idea: Place horse tokens in the square stable and see that counting 5 along each side counts every corner horse twice, so the number of horses is 20 minus the horses in the corner stalls.
tool_config.screen: A warm, colourful, polished educational-game scene: the square royal stable of 12 stalls on a soft isometric courtyard with soft shadows and gentle animation, the largest thing on screen. The 4 corner stalls are shaded in a different colour from the 8 edge stalls. Each stall shows its horses as large dots and a number. Controls: tap a stall, then + to add a horse or − to remove one (or drag a horse token from the tray), Check, Undo, Reset, Hint. Read-outs: four side counters, one beside each side (Top, Right, Bottom, Left), each adding the 4 stalls on its side and turning green when it reads 5; a total counter, Horses in the stable, that counts every horse once; a Count one by one button that lights each horse in turn with a running count; and a target card above the stable. A horse placed in a corner stall lights both of its sides. Before the stable, a small practice picture (a practice value, not from the book) shows 12 children in a ring around a square, 4 on each side; tapping a corner child lights its two sides. On every scene: Back and Next in the same place, progress dots and a Restart button.
student_does: Phase 1, Recall and get ready: a small ring of 12 children stands around a square, 4 on each side. The student taps a corner child to see two sides light up and says why adding the four sides gives more than 12.

Phase 2, Play and apply: the student places horse tokens in the stalls, watches the four side counters and the total, copies the caretaker's arrangement from the story, counts the horses one by one, and makes arrangements with no horse in any corner stall.
Phase 3, Challenge: the student arranges the 18 horses with 5 on each side, then tries fewer horses and finds how many more horses the thief can steal before the king notices something is wrong.
challenges: Phase 2, corner stall: put one horse in the top left corner stall and nowhere else. Which side counters change, and what does the total show? Answer: the Top and Left counters both show 1, but the total shows only 1 horse.

Phase 2, the caretaker's stable: place the horses as the caretaker did: top row 1, 2, 2, 0; the two middle stalls on the left 1 and 3; the two middle stalls on the right 2 and 3; bottom row 0, 2, 3, 0. Read the four side counters and the total. Answer: every side shows 5 and the total is 19.
Phase 2, count one by one: press Count one by one on the caretaker's stable. Answer: 1 + 2 + 2 + 0 + 1 + 3 + 2 + 3 + 0 + 2 + 3 + 0 = 19 horses, not 20.
Phase 2, no corner horses: put no horse in any corner stall and make every side show 5. How many horses are there? Answer: 20, because no horse is counted twice.

Phase 3, the 18 horses: The following night, the thief stole another horse from the stable. Now, only 18 horses remained. The caretaker once again cleverly arranged the 18 horses, so that there were 5 horses on each side of the square stable. How do you think he was able to do it? Arrange the 18 horses in the stable with 5 on each side. Answer: 1 horse in the top left and 1 horse in the bottom right corner stall, and 2 horses in each of the 8 middle stalls. Every side shows 5 and 1 + 1 + 8 × 2 = 18. Other arrangements can work too.

Phase 3, how many more: How many more horses can the thief steal before the king notices something is wrong? Try making the arrangements yourself. Answer: the horses = 20 − the horses in the corner stalls. With one horse in each corner stall there are 16 horses, so 2 more after the 18. Taking more means crowding the corner stalls, which the king would notice.
feedback: A horse placed in a corner stall lights both of its sides and raises both side counters by 1, while the total goes up by 1 only.
A side counter that reads 5 turns green. The total counter shows the real number of horses, each horse counted once.
Count one by one lights each horse in turn, so the student can compare the 4 sides added together with the real number of horses.
A side that does not read 5 shows how many horses it still needs, and Check says which side is short.

concepts.concept_name: King's Horses (the count), Q1

content.text:
King's Horses (the count), Q1: The king counted 5 horses along each side. "We have 5 horses along each side and there are 4 sides. So there are a total of 20 horses, your majesty," the caretaker explained. But wait, were there really 20 horses in the stable? Count the horses one by one and check! What was the mistake in the caretaker's explanation?
1. Count the top row from the left: 1 + 2 + 2 + 0 = 5.
2. Count the left side from the top corner down: 1 + 1 + 3 + 0 = 5.
3. Count the right side from the top corner down: 0 + 2 + 3 + 0 = 5.
4. Count the bottom row from the left: 0 + 2 + 3 + 0 = 5.
5. Every side shows 5, so the caretaker counted 4 × 5 = 20.
6. Now count the horses one by one, each stall once. Top row: 1 + 2 + 2 + 0 = 5. The two middle stalls on the left: 1 + 3 = 4. The two middle stalls on the right: 2 + 3 = 5. Bottom row: 0 + 2 + 3 + 0 = 5.
7. Add the four groups: 5 + 4 + 5 + 5 = 19. There are 19 horses, not 20.
8. The mistake: the horse in the top left corner stall stands on two sides, the top and the left, so it was counted twice.
9. Check: 4 × 5 − 1 = 19, with 1 corner horse counted twice.
Answer: There are 19 horses. The horse in the corner stall was counted on two sides, so 20 − 1 = 19

concepts.concept_name: King's Horses (18 horses), Q2

content.text:
King's Horses (18 horses), Q2: The following night, the thief stole another horse from the stable. Now, only 18 horses remained. The caretaker once again cleverly arranged the 18 horses, so that there were 5 horses on each side of the square stable. How do you think he was able to do it? Arrange the 18 horses in the stable with 5 on each side.
1. The caretaker counted 5 on each of the 4 sides: 4 × 5 = 20 counts.
2. Only 18 horses stand there, so 20 − 18 = 2 counts are extra.
3. Each horse in a corner stall is counted twice, so exactly 2 horses must stand in corner stalls.
4. Put 1 horse in the top left corner stall and 1 horse in the bottom right corner stall. The other two corner stalls stay empty.
5. Top side: the top left corner has 1, so the two middle stalls must hold 4. Put 2 in each: 1 + 2 + 2 + 0 = 5.
6. Right side: 0 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 5.
7. Bottom side: 1 + 2 + 2 + 0 = 5.
8. Left side: 0 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 5.
9. Count the horses one by one: 2 in the corners, and 8 middle stalls with 2 horses each, 8 × 2 = 16. Then 2 + 16 = 18.
10. Check: 4 × 5 − 2 = 18, and every side shows 5.
Answer: Put 1 horse in the top left and 1 in the bottom right corner stall, and 2 horses in each of the 8 middle stalls. Every side shows 5 and there are 18 horses. Your arrangement may differ

concepts.concept_name: King's Horses (how many more), Q3

content.text:
King's Horses (how many more), Q3: How many more horses can the thief steal before the king notices something is wrong? Try making the arrangements yourself.
1. Counting 5 along each of the 4 sides gives 4 × 5 = 20 counts.
2. A horse in a corner stall is counted twice. So the number of horses = 20 − the horses in the corner stalls.
3. 19 horses need 20 − 19 = 1 corner horse. 18 horses need 20 − 18 = 2 corner horses.
4. Fewer horses need more corner horses. 17 horses need 20 − 17 = 3. 16 horses need 20 − 16 = 4, one in each corner stall.
5. Try 16 horses with 1 horse in each corner stall. Each side already has 2 from its corners, so its two middle stalls hold 5 − 2 = 3, for example 2 and 1.
6. Top side: 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 5. The other three sides are the same. The horses are 4 + 4 × 3, and 4 × 3 = 12, so 4 + 12 = 16.
7. From 18 horses to 16 horses the thief takes 18 − 16 = 2 more.
8. To keep 5 on every side with fewer than 16 horses, a corner stall must hold more than 1 horse. Put 3, 2, 3 and 2 horses in the four corner stalls and leave the middle stalls empty. Every side shows 3 + 2 = 5 and there are 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 10 horses.
9. All the horses then crowd into the corners and the stalls between them are empty. The king would notice. The book does not print a number for this, so this is one way to read the question.
10. Check: 20 − 4 = 16 with one horse in each corner stall, and 20 − 10 = 10 with the corner stalls crowded.
Answer: 2 more horses, leaving 16 with one horse in each corner stall (horses = 20 − the horses in the corner stalls). Taking more means crowding the corner stalls, which the king would notice

Answer: There are 19 horses. The horse in the corner stall was counted on two sides, so 20 − 1 = 19

concepts.concept_name: Chapter Revision: We the Travellers - I

content.text:
1. Predict first: you have travelled through the whole chapter. Can you say one idea from each stop, from the first journey to the king's stable? Read the lines below and tick each idea you remembered.
2. Journeys: long ago people travelled on foot, on animals, and by boats and sailing ships. Today we use bicycles, motorbikes, cars, buses, trains, ships and aeroplanes, and submarines and spacecraft too.
3. Place value: 10 Ones make 1 Ten, 10 Tens make 1 Hundred, 10 Hundreds make 1 Thousand, and 10 Thousands make Ten Thousand. 9,000 + 1,000 = 10,000, written in a new column, TTh.
4. Check: which new column did the chart gain for ten thousand? The TTh column. A comma helps us read large numbers.
5. Reading and writing: say the thousands part first, then the rest, and keep every zero in its place. 10,010 is ten thousand ten, and forty thousand eight is 40,008, because 40,000 + 8 = 40,008.
6. Check: write fifty thousand five in digits. It is 50,005, with zeros in the thousands, hundreds and tens places.
7. Patterns: find the step between neighbouring numbers and test it on the next pair. 456, 567, 678 goes up by 111, because 567 − 456 = 111 and 678 − 567 = 111.
8. Comparing: more digits means a greater number. 49,014 has 5 digits and 9,990 has 4 digits, so 49,014 is greater. With the same number of digits, compare from the left.
9. Digit swap: swapping two digits changes the number. In 1,478, swapping 7 and 4 gives 1,748.
10. Expanded form: 9,123 = 9 Thousands + 1 Hundred + 2 Tens + 3 Ones, and 983 = 90 Tens + 83 Ones.
11. Check: 90 Tens is how many? It is 900, and 900 + 83 = 983.
12. Nearest numbers: the nearest ten, hundred or thousand is the neighbour that needs the fewest jumps. For 2,346, the nearest ten is 2,350, after 4 jumps.
13. In an hour a person can generally travel 3 to 5 km on foot, 12 to 20 km by cycle, 40 to 60 km by motorbike and 750 to 920 km by aircraft. For many hours, take the distance in one hour times the number of hours.
14. Large numbers around us: a book with about 200 pages, and about 50 words in each, has about 10,000 words, because 200 × 50 = 10,000.
15. Check: 200 × 5 = 1,000. Is that a 4-digit or a 5-digit count? It is a 4-digit count.
16. Puzzles: in the river puzzle, list the pairs that can be left alone, and the sheep crosses first. In the pile of pebbles, play small piles and look for what stays the same. In Mira's puzzle, write every step: the differences are all in the table of 9 and the end is 9.

17. King's Horses: counting 5 on each of 4 sides counts every corner horse twice, so the horses = 4 × 5 − the horses in the corner stalls.

objectives.objective_text: Students name the ways of travelling of long ago and of about a hundred years ago and say which is older, a boat or a bullock cart.
Students sort the ways of travelling into long ago and about a hundred years ago.
Students count in thousands from 1,000 up to 9,000, add one more thousand, and write the result as ten thousand, 10,000.
Students extend the place value chart with a TTh column, write ten thousand as 10,000 with a comma, and state the value of each digit in a number such as 9,123.
Students fill the boxes from 1,000 to 9,000, add one more thousand to write 10,000, and explain how 10 thousands make one ten thousand.
Students read a number beyond ten thousand from its tokens and its place value chart, saying the thousands part first and then the hundreds, tens and ones.
Students read numbers that have zeros in some places, such as 30,402, by saying only the places that hold a digit and skipping every place that holds a zero.
Students read the number name of five-digit numbers from tokens, charts and digits, and check each name by writing the number back from it.
Students write a number beyond ten thousand from its number name by placing the digits in the TTh, Th, H, T and O places and putting the comma before the last three digits.
Students write numbers whose names skip a place, such as forty thousand eight, by putting a zero in every empty place of the chart.
Students write numbers from their number names, fill each empty place with a zero, and check each answer by reading the number back.
Students find the rule of a number pattern by subtracting neighbouring numbers, test it on every pair, and write the next numbers.
Students continue a pattern that goes down by subtracting the same number, and a pattern that passes ten thousand, and name the rule in words.
Students find the rule of each number pattern, say whether it adds or subtracts, and fill every blank, checking the last number with the rule.
Students compare two numbers by counting their digits first, and when the digits are equal they compare place by place from the left, to say which number is greater.
Students place numbers on a number line, read them from left to right to arrange them in increasing order, and read them from right to left to arrange them in decreasing order.
Students write numbers that lie between two given numbers, including numbers whose ones, tens and hundreds digits are all zero, by keeping the leading digits and changing a later place.
Students compare and order large numbers and write numbers between two numbers in the book's questions, and explain why one number is greater by counting digits and comparing place by place.
Students swap two digits of a number, write the new number, and say whether it is bigger or smaller by finding the new value of each swapped digit.
Students swap one pair of digits to make the biggest number and the smallest number they can, by moving the biggest or the smallest digit to the leftmost place.
Students swap two digits of a number to make a number that is larger, in a given range, as small as possible or as big as possible, and compare the new number with the old one.
Students write a number in expanded form by adding the value of each digit, and leave out a zero term while the other digits keep their places.
Students find how many tens, hundreds and thousands a number holds, write it as tens plus ones, and find how many notes of 10, 100, 500 and 1,000 it makes.
Students write expanded forms, fill tens, hundreds and thousands plus ones, and count the notes of 10, 100 and 500 and the thousands in a number, in the book's questions.
Students find the nearest ten of a number by counting the jumps from the number to its two neighbouring tens and choosing the one with fewer jumps.
Students find the nearest hundred and the nearest thousand of a number by counting the jumps to the two neighbouring hundreds or thousands, and see that the two answers can differ.
Students write two numbers that have the same nearest ten, hundred or thousand, and check their choice by counting the jumps of each number to both neighbours.
Students find the nearest ten, hundred and thousand of a number by counting jumps to the two neighbouring marks, fill the table, and write numbers that have the same nearest number.
Students match a travel condition, such as a desert, a snow-covered hill, deep water or outer space, to the animal or vehicle that the book names for it.
Students read how far a person generally travels in one hour by each means of travel, say how many digits the distance has, and find which means can cover a given distance in an hour.
Students find the number of vehicles needed for a group by dividing the number of people by the number of people one vehicle carries, and check the answer by multiplying.
Students use the book's distances and vehicle sizes on a transport map to find how far a cyclist goes in 4 hours and how many vehicles carry 900 people, and check each answer.
Students estimate a large count around them by multiplying the count in one part by the number of parts, and say whether the count is a 4-digit or a 5-digit number.
Students find things in a book, a classroom, a tree and a town whose counts are 4-digit or 5-digit numbers, and explain each count by grouping and multiplying.
Students list which pairs the boatman can leave alone on a bank, use the safe pair to find the first crossing, and explain why the sheep, which is in both unsafe pairs, has to cross first.
Students play small piles of pebbles such as 2 and 2, write every move of both players, and say what stays the same after the second player's move.
Students follow Mira's subtract and repeat steps with a pair of digits they choose, write every step, and find what is common to all the differences.
Students solve the river crossing puzzle in the fewest trips, win the pile of pebbles, and explain why the differences in Mira's puzzle are in the table of 9 and the end is 9.
Students explain why counting along the four sides of a square counts each corner twice, and find the real total by subtracting the corner ones that were counted twice.
Students place the horses in the stable so that every side shows 5, count them one by one, and find how many more horses the thief can steal.

Book item: Arrange the numbers below in increasing order. You can use the number line below, if required. 40,347, 34,407, 40,473, 34,740, 73,404, 74,430, 47,340, 18,926.

Book item: The following table shows the population of some towns. Arrange them in a descending (decreasing) order. Town 1 65,232, Town 2 53,231, Town 3 56,380, Town 4 51,336, Town 5 45,858, Town 6 66,540.
Book item: Find numbers between 42,750 and 53,500 such that the ones, tens, and hundreds digits are all 0.

Book item: Digit swap. (a) In the number 1,478, interchanging the digits 7 and 4 gives 1,748. Now, interchange any two digits in the number 1,478 to make a number that is larger than 5,500. (b) Interchange two digits of 10,593 to make a number (i) between 11,000 and 15,000 (ii) more than 35,000. (c) Interchange two digits of 48,247 to make a number (i) as small as possible (ii) as big as possible.
Book item: Write the following numbers in the expanded form. One has been done for you. (a) 783 = 700 + 80 + 3 (b) 8,062 (c) 9,980 (d) 10,304 (e) 23,004 (f) 70,405.
Book item: Fill in the blanks with the correct answer. Share your thoughts in class. (a) 983 = 90 Tens + 83 Ones (b) 68 = ___ Tens + 18 Ones.

Book item: Fill in the blanks with the correct answer. (c) 607 = 4 Hundreds + ___ Ones (d) 5,621 = 4 Thousand + ___ Hundreds + 2 Tens + ___ Ones (e) 7,069 = ___ Thousand + 20 Hundreds + ___ Ones (f) 37,608 = ___ Ten Thousand + 17 Thousand + ___ Hundreds + 8 Ones (g) 43,001 = 3 Ten Thousand + ____ Thousand + ____ Hundreds + 1 Ones.

Book item: Fill in the blanks with the correct answers. (e) How many notes of ₹10 are there in ₹65,342? (f) How many notes of ₹100 are there in ₹65,342? (g) How many thousands are there in 65,342? (h) How many ₹500 notes are there in ₹65,342?

Book item: A rabbit is hungry. The rabbit is at 2,346. Its food has been kept at its neighbouring tens, 2,340 and 2,350. On which tens should the rabbit go to get its food, with the least number of steps?

Book item: The rabbit is at 2,346. Its food has been kept at its neighbouring hundreds, 2,300 and 2,400. Which of the two hundreds should the rabbit go to? ___ is the nearest hundred of 2,346. It will need ___ jumps to reach ___.

Book item: The rabbit is at 2,346. Its food has been kept at its neighbouring thousands, 2,000 and 3,000. Which number should the rabbit go to? ___ is the nearest thousand of 2,346. It will need ___ jumps to reach ___.
Book item: Fill in the boxes appropriately. Find the nearest tens, nearest hundreds and nearest thousands of 3,176, 4,017, 5,789 and 8,203.

Book item: Think and write two numbers that have the same (a) Nearest ten. (b) Nearest hundred. (c) Nearest thousand. For example, 19 and 21 have the same nearest ten, that is, 20.
Book item: Think and write the numbers that have the same (a) Nearest ten and nearest hundred. (b) Nearest hundred and nearest thousand. (c) Nearest ten, hundred and thousand.
Book item: A cyclist can cover 15 km in one hour. How much distance will she cover in 4 hours, if she maintains the same speed?

Book item: A school has 461 girls and 439 boys. How many vehicles are needed for all of them to go on a trip using the following modes of travel? The numbers in the bracket indicate the number of people that can travel in one vehicle. (a) Bicycle (2) (b) Autorickshaw (3) (c) Car (4) (d) Big car (6)

Book item: A school has 461 girls and 439 boys. How many vehicles are needed for all of them to go on a trip using the following modes of travel? The numbers in the bracket indicate the number of people that can travel in one vehicle. (e) Tempo traveller (10) (f) Boat (20) (g) Minibus (25) (h) Aeroplane (180)
Book item: A book has around 200 pages, and each page has about 50 words. About how many words does the book have in all?
Book item: Find something in the maths book whose count is a 4-digit number.
Book item: Find something in the classroom whose count is a (i) 4-digit number (ii) 5-digit number.
Book item: List some quantities whose count is a 4-digit or a 5-digit number in the context of (i) a tree (ii) your village/town/city, or any other place of your choice.

Book item: A boatman wants to cross a river in a boat. He has to take a lion, a sheep, and a bundle of grass with him. He can take one of them at a time. If the sheep and grass are left on the shore, the sheep will eat the grass. And, if the sheep and lion are left on the shore, the lion will eat the sheep. How can the boatman take the lion, sheep, and grass across the river? Help him so that he can ferry the lion, sheep, and grass across the river safely, and in the minimum number of trips.

Book item: There are two piles of pebbles. Each pile contains 7 pebbles. Each player can pick as many pebbles they want from either of the piles. The player who picks the last pebble wins. Try this game with your friends. Now, how do you play so that you win? To find a winning strategy, try playing with 1 pebble in each pile, two in each, three in each, and so on.

Book item: (a) Take any two different digits, for example 3 and 7. (b) Make two 2-digit numbers using them: 37 and 73. (c) Subtract the smaller number from the bigger number: 73 − 37 = 36. Now, use the two digits in the difference and repeat steps (b) and (c). Continue this process until you get a 1-digit number. Write the whole process.

Book item: How did Mira know what the 1-digit number in the end would be? Let us explore. (1) Observe the differences you get in each step of the process for the digits 3 and 7: 36, 27, 45 and 9. Do you notice anything in common? (2) Try the puzzle using any other pair of digits. What is common to these differences? What do you get in the end? (3) What digits can you choose so that you get a 1-digit number in the first step itself? Give some examples. Describe the pattern in the digits. (4) Now, find different digits such that the difference between the numbers is 27.

Book item: Mira found an interesting relationship between the two digits and the difference obtained. Can you see it in the table that Mira made? Digits 3, 7: 7 − 3 = 4 and 73 − 37 = 36. Digits 1, 9: 9 − 1 = 8 and 91 − 19 = 72. Digits 2, 8: 8 − 2 = 6 and 82 − 28 = 54. Digits 4, 5: 5 − 4 = 1 and 54 − 45 = 9. Extend this table by choosing appropriate digits so that the resulting differences are 2, 3, 5, and 7 respectively. What do the differences between the digits indicate?

Book item: List the numbers that give a 1-digit number in the third subtraction. Identify pairs of digits that lead to the 1-digit number after the maximum possible number of subtractions. Compare your answers with your friends.

Book item: The king counted 5 horses along each side. "We have 5 horses along each side and there are 4 sides. So there are a total of 20 horses, your majesty," the caretaker explained. But wait, were there really 20 horses in the stable? Count the horses one by one and check! What was the mistake in the caretaker's explanation?

Book item: The following night, the thief stole another horse from the stable. Now, only 18 horses remained. The caretaker once again cleverly arranged the 18 horses, so that there were 5 horses on each side of the square stable. How do you think he was able to do it? Arrange the 18 horses in the stable with 5 on each side.
Book item: How many more horses can the thief steal before the king notices something is wrong? Try making the arrangements yourself.
